en: Arjuna said:
For my benefit, [you have spoken] the supreme secret known as the Adhyātma.
By the words you have spoken, this delusion of mine has vanished.
Śrīdhara:
Having proclaimed the majesty of his divine manifestations with supreme compassion,
Hari then revealed his universal form to Arjuna, who desired to see it.
At the end of the previous chapter, the supreme form of the Lord, which is the soul of the universe, was introduced with the words: "Pervading this entire world, I remain with but one part.

Desiring to behold that [form] and rejoicing in what was previously said, Arjuna spoke in four verses beginning with "For my grace" (*mad-anugrahāya*). [The phrase] "for my grace" means for the cessation of his grief.
The supreme, secret, and even hidden teaching known as *adhyātma*— which concerns the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self—
that speech which was spoken by You beginning with "You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for" and extending up to the end of the sixth chapter;
by that, this delusion of mine— the error characterized by such thoughts as "I am the slayer" and "these are being slain"— [has been dispelled].
It has departed and perished;
for it is stated that there is an absence of agency and other such qualities in the self. //1//
Madhusūdana:

Having heard the Blessed One’s declaration in the previous chapter— after describing various manifestations— that "pervading this entire universe, I remain with but one part, the world," and having heard of that supreme form of the Lord which is the soul of the universe, Arjuna became intensely eager to perceive it directly.
Desiring what was previously mentioned and rejoicing in it, [He said]:

"For the sake of My grace—that is, for the benefit of the cessation of your grief—[I shall declare] that which is supreme, culminating in the unsurpassed goal of human life, secret (guhya)—meaning to be kept hidden, unfit to be spoken to just anyone—and designated as 'adhyātma' (relating to the self), concerning the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self; [you who], grieving for those who should not be grieved for..."

From the words "Thou art" (*tvam asi*) up to the end of the sixth chapter, that speech or statement which was spoken by You, the supremely compassionate and omniscient One— by that statement, this delusion characterized by various misconceptions, such as "I am the slayer of these" or "these are being slain by me," has departed and been destroyed for me, as witnessed by my own direct experience.
Because it has been stated there more than once that the Self is devoid of all modifications. //1//
Viśvanātha:
In the eleventh [chapter], having seen the universal form (viśvarūpa), Pārtha, his mind bewildered, offered praise; then, having shown himself once more, Hari gladdened him.

At the end of the previous chapter, having heard that the Primordial Person— the locus of all glories— is the one who stands supporting this entire universe with but a single fraction of Himself, and being a portion of His own dear friend, Arjuna is immersed in supreme bliss; desiring to behold that form,
he rejoices in what the Blessed One has said with these three verses, beginning with "By My grace."
The term *adhyātmam* is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) used in the sense of the locative case; thus, it means "within the self" (*ātmani*).
That speech in which whatever designations (*saṃjñā*) characterized by manifestations (*vibhūti*) have arisen—that is [the subject].
Delusion (*moha*) is the ignorance regarding that sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). //1//
Baladeva:
Having beheld the universal form (viśva-rūpa) in the eleventh [chapter] and being terrified in mind, Arjuna offered praise; then, having shown his own true form, Hari gladdened him.

In the previous discourse, at the commencement of the description of His manifestations (*vibhūti*)—with the words "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, dwelling in the heart of all beings"—and at its conclusion—"by Me this whole [world] is pervaded"—Arjuna understood from the Lord's own mouth that Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*), the creator of the Great Principle (*mahat*), who is the substratum of all manifestations; and that He, as the creator of the Great Principle and so forth, is the source of all incarnations. Thus, immersed in an ocean of joy through their friendship, Arjuna, desiring to behold that form of the Supreme Person, repeats what was spoken by Kṛṣṇa: "Me... [etc.].
Thus:

"The delusion of mine—which was expressed by You when You spoke those words concerning Your manifestations (vibhūti) known as the 'inner self' (adhyātma), saying 'How may I know [You]? and so forth—has departed, that is, it has been destroyed. That recognition (saṃjñā) characterized by Your manifestations, which pertains to the inner self—that is, to Yourself, the Supreme Self—has arisen."
The compound *avyayībhāva* is used in the sense of the case-ending (*vibhakty-arthe*) for that speech of his;
the meaning is that it is the supreme secret, an extreme mystery, inaccessible to anyone other than you. //1//
For the origin and dissolution of beings have been heard by me in detail from you,
O lotus-eyed one, as well as your inexhaustible majesty. (11.2)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the origin and dissolution":
I have heard from scripture that the origin and dissolution of beings—that is, their creation and reabsorption—occur solely from you.
"In the beginning, [it was said] 'I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire world,' and so forth;
furthermore, this has been stated at length again and again.
O lotus-petal-eyed one, you whose large eyes are as serene as the petals of a lotus!"
Furthermore, its majesty has been heard to be immutable and inexhaustible;
even while being the agent of the creation of the universe and so forth, the controller of all, the instigator of auspicious and inauspicious karma,
and the bestower of various fruits such as bondage and liberation, it is characterized by changelessness, non-differentiation, non-attachment, and indifference.
And His immeasurable greatness has been heard: "The unintelligent think of Me, who am unmanifest, as having attained manifestation";
"All this is pervaded by Me";
and "Yet those actions do not bind Me."

By such statements as "I am equal toward all beings," the sense is that my delusion— such as the thought "I am the agent"— which arose from the belief that living beings are dependent upon me, has now vanished. //2//
Madhusūdana:

Likewise, he says "bhavāpyayau" (origination and dissolution) to indicate that from the seventh chapter up to the tenth, he has heard the Lord’s words, which primarily consist of the determination of the meaning of that word (*tat-pada*).
The meaning is: the origination and dissolution—the birth and death—of beings proceed from you alone; these have been heard by me from you in detail, and not merely in brief or only once.

O lotus-eyed one, you whose eyes are long like lotus petals, red at the corners, and supremely beautiful— this description of the excellence of your extreme beauty is due to the intensity of [our] love.
Not only have the origin and dissolution of the world been heard from you, O Great-Souled One, but also your disposition, your majesty, and your supreme sovereignty.

The phrase "and so forth" (*ca-kārāt*) follows the completed thought: "I have heard from You that, even while being the agent of the creation of the universe and so on, You remain changeless; even while causing beings to perform auspicious and inauspicious actions, You remain impartial; even while bestowing diverse fruits such as bondage and liberation, You remain unattached and indifferent; and furthermore, Your nature as the Self of all, whether with attributes (*sopādhika*) or without attributes (*nirupādhika*), is imperishable and undecaying. //2//
Viśvanātha:

In this group of six verses, however, [the Lord declares] that "origination and dissolution—creation and withdrawal—proceed from You," and "I am the source and likewise the dissolution of the entire world," and so forth; thus He describes His inexhaustible majesty, characterized by the absence of attachment to authority and the like, even while acting as the agent of creation and other cosmic functions.
"By Me all this is pervaded," and "yet those actions do not bind Me," and so forth. //2//
Baladeva: Furthermore, what do you say?
O lotus-petal-eyed one!
This description of his supreme beauty is due to the intensity of [my] love, for his eyes have long, reddish corners that are exceedingly beautiful, like the petals of a lotus.
From you— from your presence— I have heard repeatedly and in detail that the origin and dissolution of beings, their creation and destruction, proceed from you;

and [I have heard] your imperishable and eternal majesty and sovereignty, as well as your state of being changeless despite being the creator of all, and your state of being the controller of all— as expressed in such passages as, "I am the source and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe."
Such qualities as "being unattached" and so forth have been heard by me from you yourself in detail, through such statements as "all this is pervaded by Me. //2//
"It is even so as you have described yourself, O Supreme Lord.
I desire to see your divine form, O Supreme Person."
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, "this is indeed so," because I have heard [from you] that "the origin and dissolution of beings," and so forth;
and now you speak thus, O Supreme Lord: "Pervading this entire world, I stand with but a single fraction."
It is even so;
here too, I have no lack of faith.
Nevertheless, O Supreme Person, out of curiosity I wish to see that form of Yours, which is endowed with sovereignty, power, valor, and splendor. //3//
Madhusūdana:

O Supreme Lord, in whatever manner—whether as possessing attributes (*sopādhika*) or as being devoid of attributes (*nirupādhika*)—You describe Yourself as having unsurpassed sovereignty, it is exactly so and not otherwise.
The meaning is that there is no suspicion whatsoever in me regarding any lack of confidence in Your word.

Even though this is so, nevertheless, desiring to become one who has accomplished his purpose, I wish to see your divine form, endowed with knowledge, sovereignty, power, strength, valor, and splendor—wondrous, O Puruṣottama! By this address, he indicates: "I have no lack of faith in your word, and a great desire to see exists within me"; for you know this through your omniscience and because you are the inner controller of all. //3//

Viśvanātha: Now, regarding what you have said of yourself—"I stand supporting this entire world with but a single portion"—the sense is that it is exactly so for me; there is no lack of conviction here at all.

But even that [form] having its purpose withdrawn, I desire to see Your divine form through the longing to behold it—that form by which, as a single portion of the Lord's nature, You exist pervading the universe;
the meaning is that I now wish to see that very form of Yours with my own eyes. //3//
Baladeva said: "So be it. Regarding that Self which You describe with the words "I, having pervaded this," etc., that is indeed exactly so;

there is not even a trace of doubt in me concerning that. Nevertheless, O Supreme Lord, O Puruṣottama—addressing You thus because You surely know my desire to see that form—I wish to behold Your divine form as the ruler of all out of curiosity.
It expresses: "Fill that [desire].
The meaning is: for me, who has tasted your sweetness, a longing to experience your sovereignty arises, just as one who has tasted a sweet flavor might desire to take up a bitter one. //3//
O Lord, O Master of Yoga, if you think it is possible for me to see that [form], then show me your imperishable self. (11.4)
Śrīdhara: It is not by the mere statement "I do not wish to see" that you must show that form; what then? [The Lord says,] "You think so.
For the yogis themselves are the yogas.
He is the Lord of them.
If you think that it is possible for me, Arjuna, to behold that form, then show me your own self, which possesses that form—imperishable and eternal. 4.
Madhusūdana says "manyase" (you think) out of suspicion as to how you can have a desire to see that which is unfit to be seen.
He is called *prabhu* because he has power (*prabhavati*) over creation, maintenance, destruction, entry, and governance.
O Lord, O Sovereign of All—
if You think, that is, if You know or desire, that this divine form of Yours can be seen by me, Arjuna;
O Lord of Yoga, O Master of all yogis who possess the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth— then, by virtue of Your will:

Thus, since I have entreated you so fervently, you, who are supremely compassionate, show yourself—make yourself the object of my visual knowledge—in your imperishable and undecaying form, distinguished by divine majesty. //4//
Viśvanātha:
By the term "O Lord of Yoga," the sense is that even for one such as myself who is unworthy, it is precisely your mastery of yoga (*yogaiśvarya*) that is the cause for my fitness to behold Him. //4//
Baladeva: In the vision of His sovereignty, he seeks the Lord’s consent with the words "if You so deem it" (*manyase yadi*). The meaning is: "Do You know [it]? or "Do You wish [it]?
O Lord, O Sovereign of all!
By addressing him as "O Lord of Yoga," he suggests that for an unworthy person like me, your very power is the sole cause for beholding you. //4//
The Blessed Lord said: Behold, O Pārtha, my forms by the hundreds and by the thousands.
Various kinds of divine [objects], of diverse colors and forms. //5//

Śrīdhara: Being thus entreated, the Blessed Lord, wishing to show His most wondrous form, addresses Arjuna with "Behold! in four verses to draw him toward Him, saying, "Be attentive. Although the form is one, the plural "forms" (*rūpāṇi*) is used because it consists of many varieties;
they are immeasurable and of manifold kinds.
Behold my divine, supramundane forms;
their colors are white, black, and so forth;
their shapes are specific arrangements of parts.
Those which possess various and manifold colors and shapes are "nānā-varṇākṛtīni. //5//
Madhusūdana:

Being thus entreated by Arjuna, who was his most devoted follower, the Blessed Lord said, "Behold. Here, by repeating the word "behold" throughout the sequence of these four verses, the Lord draws Arjuna’s attention toward Him, intending to show him forms of such extreme wonder, and saying, "Be attentive."

Behold my forms—by the hundreds and by the thousands, indeed immeasurable; diverse and of many kinds, divine and most wonderful; possessing various distinct colors such as blue, yellow, and other celestial types, as well as various shapes and specific arrangements of limbs.
Behold these my forms of manifold colors and shapes.
The suffix *loṭ* is used for the sense of "fitness.
O Pārtha, become one who is fit to see. //5//
Viśvanātha:

And therefore, I first display this form of my own partial incarnation, the First Person who is the inner controller of primordial nature (prakṛti), as described in the Puruṣasūkta: "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet. I show this form first.

Thinking to himself, "Later, for the sake of what is relevant to the present topic, I shall also make known that very [Self] as being Time," he addresses Arjuna, drawing his attention by saying, "Behold! and "My forms. Even within my single essential nature, there are hundreds of my essential natures, which are my divine manifestations (vibhūtayaḥ). //5//

Baladeva: Thus entreated, the Blessed One, for the sake of the present context, spoke the word "Behold" four times, intending to make Arjuna attentive so as to manifest his own partial incarnation (svāṃśa) in the form of a deity— namely, the inner controller (antaryāmin) of Prakṛti, who possesses a thousand heads and is preeminent in sovereignty— and to make him understand that [form] therein is also of the nature of Time (kālātmaka).
The repetition of the word "paśya" (behold) should be understood as intended to highlight the extreme wonder of the forms that are to be seen.

"Me," meaning mine—of me alone, appearing in the form of a thousand heads—behold hundreds and thousands of forms that constitute my manifestations. The imperative mood here denotes fitness; the sense is: "you are worthy to ask about them. (BhG 11.6)
Behold the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and likewise the Maruts;
behold, O Bhārata, many wonders never seen before! (6)
Śrīdhara: "Behold those very ones"—behold the sun and the others within my body;
behold the Maruts, the forty-nine specific deities.
Forms never seen before by you or by anyone else—wonders, marvelous things. //6//
Madhusūdana, having said,
"Behold the divine forms," proceeds to describe them briefly in two verses with the word "behold":
behold the twelve Ādityas, the eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the Maruts, seven groups of seven, making forty-nine.
The meaning is that [he saw] other gods as well. O Bhārata, behold many other wonders and marvels never seen before— that is, not previously seen in the world of men by you, or by anyone else.

In this context, "by the hundreds and by the thousands" is the explanation for "of various kinds"; "many" refers to [the phrase] "suns and so forth. It should be understood that "never seen before" explains "divine," and "wondrous" explains "of various colors and forms. //6//

Viśvanātha: Nothing. Baladeva: Moreover, behold right now within my body the entire universe, including all moving and non-moving beings, situated together in one place—something that could not be seen even in ten thousand years by you as you wandered here and there.
The meaning is: "Behold [them] all at once and in one place by my grace.

Furthermore, behold also that which is the support of the world—the nature of the causes such as *pradhāna* and *mahat*—as well as my own victory, defeat, and other such matters, for I desire to see them. //6//
Behold today, O Guḍākeśa, the entire universe with its moving and non-moving beings situated here in one place within my body, and whatever else you wish to see. (11.7)

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "all here in one place": behold now, at this very moment, the entire universe together with all moving and non-moving beings—which could not be seen even in tens of millions of years by one wandering here and there—abiding right here within my body, situated as a single whole in the form of its constituent parts.

Furthermore, whatever else you wish to see— the nature of the cause that serves as the substratum of the world, the specific states of the world and so forth, victory and defeat, and whatever else there may be— all that Madhusūdana [will show];
indeed, it is not merely this much.

"You ought to see even the entire world situated within my body," he says with the words "ekastham iha" (situated here in one). "Iha" means in this, my body; "ekastham" means situated in just one [place], existing in the form of a single limb; "jagat" means the whole, the entire world, including all moving and unmoving things—that is, together with everything mobile and immobile—even by wandering here and there for thousands of millions of years.
That which was impossible to see even now, behold it this very day, O Guḍākeśa!
And whatever else you wish to see, such as victory, defeat, and so forth—that too, behold, for the sake of destroying your doubt. //7//
Viśvanātha:
Even by wandering for ten million years, you would be unable to see the entire world;
yet here, within even a single part of my body, it exists all at once in one place.
And whatever else there may be, such as my own victory or defeat, within this body which is the causal form that serves as the refuge of the world. //7//
Baladeva said: "Moreover, behold right now, this very day, the entire universe with its moving and non-moving beings, situated as one within a single part of my body.
The meaning is: that which you have been unable to see even after wandering here and there for ten thousand years—behold all of that at once and in one place alone by my grace.

And whatever else you wish to see—the nature of the causal principles such as Pradhāna and Mahat which constitute the support of the universe, as well as your own victory, defeat, and so forth—that too, behold. (7)
But you are not able to see Me with this very eye of yours;
I give you a divine eye; behold My sovereign yoga. (8)
Śrīdhara: Regarding what Arjuna said, "If you think that [this form] is possible for me to see," he replies with the words "But not by this...
By means of this very physical eye of yours, it is not possible for you to see Me; you will not be capable of doing so.
Therefore, I give to you a divine, super-mundane eye consisting of knowledge.
Behold my sovereign, extraordinary yoga—the power of accomplishment through the impossible. //8//
Madhusūdana:
Regarding what was said—"if you think that it is possible for me to see"—He provides this qualification: "but not Me.
By this very natural eye, the eye established by one's own nature, you are not able—that is, you simply cannot—see Me in My divine form.
In the reading *śakyase*, the meaning is "you will not be able.
Alternatively, although *śak* belongs to the *su-ādi* (tudādi) class, the *śyan* suffix [of *śakyase*] is Vedic;
or rather, its inclusion in the *div-ādi* class is the traditional view.

"In that case, how could I be able to see You? To this He says: "I give to you, my divine eye—divine meaning non-material, capable of beholding My divine form. With that divine eye, behold My yoga: the supreme power of the Lord, My own unique capacity to bring about the impossible. (8)
Viśvanātha:

O Arjuna, do not think that Indra is a magical illusion (*indrajāla*) or a form consisting of *māyā*; rather, his true nature (*svarūpa*) consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), containing the entire universe within itself. It is for the purpose of instilling faith in him as being truly beyond the reach of the senses that he says, "But not... (*na tu*).
"You are not able—that is, you cannot—see me in my form as a mass of consciousness with these very eyes of yours, which are natural and material; therefore, I give you a divine, non-material eye.
It is precisely for the sake of causing some wonder in Arjuna, who considers himself an ordinary man, that he sees by means of that [eye].
For Arjuna, being a chief attendant of the Blessed One and an incarnation of a human, is not like an ordinary man with physical eyes."

Furthermore, what logic is there in saying that Arjuna—who directly perceives with his own eyes the very sweetness of the Lord—would need to accept divine vision because he was unable to see the Lord’s partial manifestation (aṃśa)? Some, however, explain it thus: [Arjuna] was a perceiver solely of the great sweetness of the Lord’s human pastimes.

Whatever is most excellent, that eye—like one devoted to nothing else—does not at all perceive the divine playfulness (*deva-līlātva*) and the perfection of the Blessed One; for indeed, a tongue that has tasted the flavor of camphor is unable to taste sugar-candy or molasses.

Therefore, desiring to cause Arjuna to grasp that divine, superhuman [form] which is favorable to the nectar of love (*prema-rasa*), so as to grant him that specific wonder he had requested, the Blessed One [revealed His] divine sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
"He gave sight"—thus, the intention to bestow the divine eye (divya-cakṣus) will become manifest at the end of the chapter. //8//

Baladeva says: "If you think that [what was requested] is possible, then, while fulfilling Arjuna's request, the Blessed Lord gave him divine vision capable of perceiving His own divine form in order to make him wonder; thus He said, 'But Me...

By this very [vision], which perceives exclusively My sweetness, you are not able—you cannot—simultaneously to behold Me with Your own eyes as I appear with a thousand heads, resembling a thousand suns shining at once.
Therefore, I give you divine vision;
the sense is that just as I myself manifest my own self which is overwhelmed by the supreme flow, so too shall your vision.

By that [vision], behold my sovereign yoga-form (*yoga-rūpa*); for according to its etymology, "yoga" means that by which one is joined, and from what follows, this refers to the sovereign, supreme form.

It should be understood that here only the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) was granted, and not the divine mind (*divya-manas*) as well. For if such a mind had been granted, there would have been the possibility of his taking pleasure in that [universal] form; thus, by the sign of granting the divine vision in this instance, those who claim that the universal form with a thousand heads is superior to the form of Pārtha’s charioteer—[that claim is refuted].
It should be cast away at the front. //8//
Sanjaya said:
Having spoken thus, O King, Hari, the great Lord of Yoga, then—
He revealed his supreme sovereign form to Pārtha.
Śrīdhara: Having spoken thus, the Blessed One revealed His true form to Arjuna.
Seeing that form, Arjuna made a request to Śrī Kṛṣṇa; this matter Sañjaya spoke to Dhṛtarāṣṭra in six verses beginning with "Having spoken thus" (*evam uktvā*).
O King Dhṛtarāṣṭra!
And that Hari, the great Lord of Yoga, has displayed His supreme sovereign form. //9//

Madhusūdana revealed his divine form to Arjuna. Having seen it, Arjuna was overcome with wonder and addressed the Blessed One; this account Saṃjaya related to Dhṛtarāṣṭra by saying "having spoken thus," and so forth, in these six verses beginning with that phrase.

"In this way, you cannot see Me with this [physical] eye; I shall give you divine vision. Having said this, immediately after granting that divine vision, He said: "O King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, be steady for the sake of hearing.
Hari, the Great Lord of Yoga—He who is both great and the supreme Lord of Yoga—is the remover of all afflictions for His devotees."
The Blessed One revealed to Pārtha, his singular devotee, his supreme divine sovereign form, even though it was unfit to be seen. 9.
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: Having spoken thus, Hari showed the universal form (viśvarūpa) to Pārtha;
and having beheld that form, Pārtha made this request to Hari—this is the matter that Sañjaya has related in these six verses.
Then, immediately after bestowing the divine eye, [He said]: "O King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Hari is both great and the Lord of Yoga. (9)
Having many mouths and eyes, displaying many wonders, adorned with many divine ornaments, and wielding many uplifted divine weapons. (11.10)
Wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with divine perfumes and unguents, the Lord is composed of all wonders—endless and facing in every direction. //11//
Śrīdhara: In what manner was it? To this he says: "having many mouths and eyes.
That is, that in which there are many mouths and many eyes.
That in which there is the sight of many wonders;
that in which there are many divine ornaments;
that in which there are many divine weapons raised aloft. //10//
Furthermore, regarding the word *divya*:
it is that which wears divine garlands and garments;
likewise, it is that which has such a divine fragrance as its unguent.
Consisting of all wonders, abounding in manifold marvels; divine, having the nature of illumination;
infinite, being unlimited.
That in which faces are on all sides, that is, everywhere. //11//
Madhusūdana [explains that he] qualifies that very form with the word "aneka" (many):
that form in which there are many mouths and eyes.
That in which there was the sight of many wonders that cause amazement;
that in which there were many divine ornaments and decorations;
and that which contained many divine, raised weapons and missiles—such was it.

It is "bearing divine garlands and garments" because it wears celestial garlands made of flowers and jewels, as well as divine raiment and clothes. It is "possessing divine fragrance" because its unguent has a celestial scent. It is "consisting of all wonders," meaning it abounds in many marvels.
"Divine" means having the nature of light.
"Infinite" means undivided. "Having faces on all sides" means that in which there are faces everywhere; this is to be connected with the preceding [verse], meaning "He showed that form.
Alternatively, one may supply the words "Arjuna saw. (10–11)
Viśvanātha:
That which has faces on all sides, from every direction. //11//

Baladeva: [The word] "aneka" means that form which possesses many thousands of mouths and eyes, as indicated by the subsequent statement, "Become thousand-armed, O Universal Form. Here, the words "aneka," "bahu," and "sahasra" signify "innumerable," as evidenced by such scriptural passages as, "With eyes on all sides and faces on all sides."

That [vision] wherein there was the sight of many wonders; wherein there was a divine fragrance and such anointing as that; [He who saw] the Divine, the radiant, the infinite, the boundless, whose faces were on all sides, everywhere. //10-11//
If the light of a thousand suns were to blaze forth simultaneously in the sky, that might resemble the radiance of that Great-Souled One. (11.12)

Śrīdhara: He states the incomparability of the radiance of the universal form with the words "In heaven" (*divi*). In the divine ether, if there were the simultaneous radiance of a thousand suns rising at once, even that would only somehow [resemble] the radiance of the Great-Souled One’s universal form.
It would have to be similar;
the meaning is that there is simply no other comparison.
"He displayed such a wondrous form" is to be construed with what precedes. //12//

Madhusūdana explains what was called "the god" by saying "in heaven": "In heaven," that is, in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), [as if] a thousand suns—that is, an immeasurable multitude of suns—were to rise simultaneously. Simultaneously...

If the light that has arisen—meaning the radiance—should exist, then it might perhaps be equal or similar to the light, the brilliance, of that Great-Souled One who possesses the universal form; or it might not. Even so, I believe that the light of the Universal Form itself would surely surpass it.
The meaning is that there is simply no other comparison whatsoever.

Here, because there is a determination of what is non-existent, the *ārūpeya* hyperbole (*atiśayokti*)—consisting of the absence of comparison due to that non-existence and the form of an extraordinary comparison (*abhūtopamā*)—manifests the figure of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), thereby revealing in every way the very state of being beyond comparison, as in the verse beginning "If the two [rivers] were separate streams in the sky," and so forth. //12//
Viśvanātha:

If light—that is, radiance—should arise at one and the same time, then it might somehow be similar to the light, the splendor, or the radiance of that Great-Souled One, the Cosmic-Formed Person. //12//
Baladeva: He states the incomparability of that radiance with the words "In heaven" (*divi*).

If the splendor—that is, the light—of a thousand suns rising simultaneously in the sky (*divi*, meaning the atmosphere) were to arise at once, then it might be similar to the single radiance, the single light, of that Great-Souled Hari in his universal form (*viśvarūpa*). Such is the meaning.
The present tense (*laṭ*) is used here in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*).
This is called an "extraordinary simile" (*adbhutopamā*), which,
when functioning as a poetic suggestion (*vyaṅgya*), in every way manifests the incomparability of her beauty.
"He displayed such a form"—this is the connection with what precedes. //12//
Then, O Pāṇḍava, he beheld the entire universe, divided into many parts, situated within the body of that God of gods. (11.13)

Śrīdhara: In response to the inquiry as to what occurred after that, Sañjaya says "There" (tatra). At that time, Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu, beheld the entire world—divided into many parts and existing in various divisions—situated within the body of the God of gods, standing together as its very limbs in one place alone. //13//
Madhusūdana:

Arjuna has indeed experienced what was commanded by the Blessed One—"Behold today the entire universe, with its moving and non-moving beings, standing here in one place"—as he says there, "standing in one place" (*tatraikastham*).
"Standing in one place" means situated in one location; the entire universe, though divided in many ways.

Then, in that state of beholding the wonderful universal form, the Pāṇḍava Arjuna saw within the body of the Blessed One, the God of gods, various kinds of beings such as gods, ancestors, and humans; at that moment, he saw the Universal Lord:
therein, within the very body of the God of gods on that field of battle, the entire world—the whole cosmic egg—meaning everything that is impossible to enumerate.

"Divided" means existing separately and individually; "situated in one place" means located in a single spot, such as being situated in every pore or situated in every cavity of the body—this is the meaning.
"In many ways" means made of clay, gold, or jewels, measuring fifty crores of yojanas, a hundred crores of yojanas, or a hundred thousand crores of yojanas and so forth—this is the meaning.
Baladeva says: in response to the expectation of what happened after that, he says "therein."

There on that battlefield, the son of Pāṇḍu then beheld the entire universe—the whole cosmic egg—within the manifested body of Kṛṣṇa, the God of gods, which possessed a thousand heads and was his glorious form (śrī-vigraha).
It was seen as it had been before: all existing separately yet situated in one place.
The phrase "in many ways" (anekadhā) means that the worlds were composed of clay, gold, or jewels, and existed as small, medium, or large. //13//
Then Dhananjaya, overcome with wonder and his hair standing on end,
bowed his head to the God and spoke with palms joined in reverence. (11.14)
Śrīdhara: Having seen this, what did he do?
To that, he says "tataḥ" (then), meaning immediately after that vision.
Overcome— that is, pervaded— by wonder, Dhanañjaya, whose hair stood on end with thrill,
bowed his head to that very God and, having joined his palms in reverence,
spoke as follows. //14//
Madhusūdana:
Even upon seeing such a marvel, Arjuna did not become afraid, nor did he even blink his eyes; nor, out of agitation, did he forget what ought to be done.
Nor did he depart from that place;
rather, because of his extreme fortitude, he conducted himself exactly as was appropriate for that occasion,
even amidst a great agitation of the mind— thus he says, "Then."
Then, immediately upon seeing that, he was overcome— that is, pervaded— by wonder, by the power of that marvelous vision, and by a particular, extraordinary mental thrill.

Consequently, with his hair standing on end in thrill, Dhananjaya— whose great prowess was renowned for his victories in the battle against Mahadeva and elsewhere, and who had conquered all kings at King Yudhisthira’s Rajasuya sacrifice and during the seizure of the cattle to bring back wealth— was filled with such great valor.
Or rather, because of his great majesty, he was like Agni himself,

the three-eyed one; having bowed down with his head touching the ground to that very god Nārāyaṇa who assumes all forms, and having prostrated himself with an excellence of devotion and faith, he spoke with palms joined in reverence.

In this context, through the nourishment (*paripoṣa*) of the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) called wonder (*vismaya*) residing in Arjuna—by means of the objective determinant (*ālambanavibhāva*) which is the Blessed One; the excitant determinant (*uddīpanavibhāva*) which is the vision of the Universal Form (*viśvarūpa*) seen repeatedly; the consequent determinants (*anubhāva*) such as the physical manifestation of horripilation (*sāttvikaromaharṣa*), prostration, and the gesture of joined palms; and the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as fortitude, discernment, joy, and reflection, which are either explicitly mentioned or implied by the consequent determinants—a corresponding aesthetic wonder (*cittacamatkāra*) arises in the minds of the listeners who possess the necessary latent predispositions (*savāsanā*).

It is indicated that even this [state], having reached its full development through the non-determination of those distinctions, becomes the marvelous rasa (*adbhuta-rasa*) in the form of the relish of supreme bliss. //14//
Viśvanātha: Nothing.

Baladeva: Thus, Arjuna, who knew the true nature of Kṛṣṇa, having now beheld that thousand-headed form perceived through his [inner] being, experienced a wonderful rasa; this is what he says with the word "tataḥ" (then).
The meaning is: "having beheld that Kṛṣṇa whose form was thus manifested."

"O Dhanañjaya!"—though steadfast, he was overcome with wonder; his hair standing on end and bristling with joy, he bowed his head to the ground before the Lord and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke.
Here, there was no closing of the eyes out of fear or the like on his part; rather, it is indicated that the sentiment of wonder (*adbhuta-rasa*) arose.

In this context, such a Hari is the *ālambana* (the objective basis), the repeated gazing upon Him is the *uddīpana* (the excitant), and prostration and the joining of hands are the *anubhāvas* (consequent effects).
Horripilation is a *sāttvika* emotion; by these, the mind is seized, and mental states such as fortitude and joy become transitory (*sañcārī*).
The *adbhuta-rasa* (the marvelous sentiment) is that in which the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of wonder is nourished by these factors, beginning with the objective basis (*ālambana*). //14//
BhG 11.15 Arjuna said:
O God, I see the gods within Your body.
Likewise, all the hosts of various beings,
Brahmā the Lord seated upon the lotus-throne,
all the sages, and the divine serpents— [he beheld them all]. //15//
Śrīdhara: He speaks of his vision itself in seventeen verses beginning with "I see.
O Lord, in Your body I see the gods, such as the Ādityas and others.
Likewise, [he perceives] all the various classes of beings, both stationary and moving, in their diverse forms and groups;

and likewise Brahmā, the four-faced Lord, the ruler of all, seated upon his lotus-throne— the one seated in the center of the earth-lotus upon the Meru-anther-throne, or rather, seated upon the lotus-navel-throne of the Blessed One.

Likewise, I see all the sages, such as Vasiṣṭha and others who are the sons of Brahmā, as well as the divine and ordinary serpents, headed by Vāsuki; this construction applies throughout the verse. //15//
Madhusūdana:

Arjuna spoke, saying "I see," thus manifesting his own experience: "Aha! What supreme fortune is mine, that I behold with the divine eye granted by the Blessed One even that universal form shown by the Blessed One, which is invisible to all the worlds!"

O Lord, I see and perceive with visual knowledge all the gods, beginning with the Vasus, within Your body which is the universal form; likewise, I see the multitudes and assemblies of various kinds of beings, both stationary and moving; and likewise, I see Brahmā, the four-faced Lord and ruler of all, seated upon his lotus-throne, situated in the center of the earth-lotus upon the Meru-anther-seat, seated upon the lotus-throne of the Lord’s navel.
Or thus:
"I see all the sages, such as Vasiṣṭha and others who are sons of Brahmā, and divine serpents, both ordinary and those headed by Vāsuki"—this is to be connected with every instance. //15//
Viśvanātha:
[He beheld] the multitudes of various beings, such as those born from a womb and so forth;
[and he beheld] Brahmā, seated upon the lotus-throne, situated on Mount Sumeru at the pericarp of the earth-lotus. //15//
Baladeva said: He describes what he spoke with seventeen verses beginning with "I see.

Thus, I see the multitudes of various beings, such as those born from a womb and so forth; I see Brahmā, the four-faced one, seated upon his lotus-throne; I see the Lord who dwells within him as its inner controller; and I see the wide-striding serpents, Vāsuki and others, reclining in the waters of the cosmic egg. (15)
I see You on all sides with infinite forms, possessing many arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes.
O Lord of the Universe, O Universal Form, I see neither your end, nor your middle, nor again your beginning.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the word "aneka" (many):
I see you as one who possesses many arms and other limbs;
I see you on all sides as one whose forms are infinite.
I do not perceive you as "you" nor that [object] as "that," nor even the middle or the beginning. //16//
Madhusūdana:
He further qualifies that very body of the Blessed One in which he saw all this, with the words "aneka" (many), etc.
I see you with many arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes—he who possesses many arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes. I see you on all sides, everywhere, he whose forms are infinite.
But as for you, moreover, because of your omnipresence, I do not see your end, nor your middle, nor even your beginning.
"O Lord of the Universe! O You of Universal Form!"—these two vocatives are used out of extreme agitation. //16//
Viśvanātha: O Viśveśvara, Primordial Person! //16//
Baladeva: He qualifies that body in which he saw the gods and others with the words "aneka... (many...).
O Viśvarūpa, O Primordial Person! //16//
Wearing a crown, holding a mace, and bearing a discus,
he was a mass of splendor, radiant on all sides.
I behold you, difficult to gaze upon, with the immeasurable splendor of a blazing fire and the sun on all sides. //17//
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "kirīṭinam" (wearing a crown): *kirīṭinam* means possessing a crown (*mukuṭavantam*);
*gadinaṃ* means possessing a mace (*gadāvantam*).
He possesses a discus and is endowed with wheels;
he is radiant on all sides, having the form of a mass of splendor, and is likewise difficult to behold, impossible to look upon.
The reason for this is that his radiance and brilliance are like the luster of a blazing fire and the sun.
Therefore, although You are immeasurable and impossible to determine as being "thus," I behold You on every side. //17//
Madhusūdana further qualifies that very Lord of universal form in another way as "kirīṭinam" (wearing a crown).
He is the wearer of a crown, a mace, and a discus, and he is radiant on all sides— a mass of splendor.
Therefore, it is difficult to behold; it is impossible to perceive without the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
In the reading that includes the letter *sa* (*sayakāra*), the word *duḥ* signifies negation;
that is to say, it means "unbeholdable" (*anirīkṣya*).

I see with my divine eye that which is immeasurable—that is, impossible to delimit—whose splendor is like the radiance of a blazing fire and the sun; therefore, there is no contradiction in saying that I see it as difficult to behold due to the difference in the capacity of the observer. //17//
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: He describes Him in another way as "the one wearing a crown" (*kirīṭinam*).
Even though You are difficult to behold, I see You through His grace, by means of obtaining divine vision.
The reason why [the Buddha] is difficult to behold is stated as "blazing with fire on all sides";
this [body] is immeasurable, meaning it is impossible to measure it as being "thus" or "in this way. //17//
You are the supreme imperishable to be known;
you are the ultimate abode of this universe.
You are the imperishable protector of the eternal dharma; you are considered by me to be the ancient Puruṣa. 18.
Śrīdhara: Since your sovereignty is thus, therefore you are [the Supreme].
You alone are the Imperishable, the Supreme Brahman.
Of what nature is it?
This should be known—that is, understood—by those seeking liberation:
you alone are the supreme repository of this entire universe; a "repository" (nidhāna) is that in which something is deposited, meaning the preeminent support.
Therefore, you are the imperishable and eternal one;
the protector and guardian of the eternal and constant Dharma;
the ancient and primordial Person.
You are approved by me; you are esteemed by me. //18//
Madhusūdana:
From this observation of your inconceivable and unsurpassed sovereignty,
I infer that you are indeed the Supreme Brahman, the Imperishable (akṣara), who is to be known by those seeking liberation through the hearing of the Vedāntas and other means.
You alone are the supreme, most excellent support (*nidhāna*)—that in which this universe is deposited—of this entire world;
for this very reason, You are the imperishable and eternal.
You are the protector and guardian of this eternal Dharma, which is to be propounded by the eternal Vedas.
Or, "Śāśvata" may be a vocative address.
In that case, it means "the imperishable," being devoid of destruction;
therefore, you are known and recognized by me as that very Puruṣa, the Supreme Self, who is eternal and ancient. 18.
Viśvanātha:
That which is to be known—that imperishable reality of Brahman which is to be realized by the liberated—is the treasure-store, the place of dissolution. //18//
Baladeva says: "By beholding His inconceivable and great sovereignty, I conclude that You are indeed thus," and so he says "You.

Now, that which is to be known through Vedic texts such as, "Then there is the higher [knowledge] by which that Imperishable is attained" [Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.5–6], and "That which is invisible... and so forth, is the Supreme, accompanied by Śrī.

You alone are the imperishable syllable (*akṣara*), the very treasure-trove, the refuge, and the immutable; you are the indestructible protector of the eternal Dharma, the guardian of the Dharma declared in the Vedas.

You are that ancient Puruṣa, described in the words of the mantra: "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of causes; there is no progenitor of him, nor is there any lord over him" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.9). //18//
Without beginning, middle, or end, of infinite power and infinite arms, with the moon and sun as his eyes.
I see you with a face like a blazing fire, scorching this entire universe with your own splendor. //19//
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the word "anādi":
it is without beginning, middle, or end, meaning it is devoid of origination, maintenance, and dissolution;
it is "of infinite power," meaning that whose power and majesty are infinite.
I behold you, whose arms are infinite and powerful, whose eyes are the moon and the sun,
and whose mouths have the blazing fire as their radiance.
I see this entire universe being scorched by its own splendor. //19//
Madhusūdana:
Furthermore, regarding the word "anādi" (without beginning):
the beginning is origination, the middle is persistence, and the end is destruction; that which is devoid of these is "without beginning, middle, or end."
He whose vigor and power are infinite;
he whose arms are infinite—
this is an elliptical expression that also includes his faces and other limbs.

I behold you, whose eyes are the moon and the sun; whose face is the blazing fire—or rather, who has fire in his mouths—and who, by your own splendor, heats this entire universe, causing it to burn. //19//
Viśvanātha:
Furthermore, in the statement "anādi" (beginningless), there is no fault of tautology in the speech of Arjuna, who is submerged in an ocean of the rasa of great wonder; as it is said:
"In cases of favor, wonder, or joy, what is spoken twice or thrice does not constitute a defect. (19)

Baladeva said: "Anādi" means that which is devoid of beginning, middle, and end; [he is] the one whose arms are infinite—that is, possessing a thousand arms—and whose eyes are like the moon and the sun, [belonging to him] who possesses endless heroic powers and all six sovereign lordships (aiśvarya) as his distinguishing marks.
The meaning is that his eyes were gracious toward the gods and others who bowed down, while they were cruel toward their opposites, such as the asuras.
He is the one whose faces resemble blazing fires and are conducive to the act of withdrawal (saṃhāra).
In Arjuna’s speech, occasional repetition is not a fault, because he was overcome with wonder.
As it has been said: "In cases of clarity, astonishment, or joy, what is spoken two or three times does not constitute a fault. (19)
For this space between heaven and earth,
as well as all the directions, are pervaded by you alone.
O Great-Souled One, having seen this wondrous and fierce form of yours, the three worlds are deeply distressed.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "of heaven and earth":
this intermediate space between heaven and earth has been pervaded by you alone;
and all the directions have also been pervaded.
It is marvelous, never seen before.
Having seen this fierce and terrible form of yours, the three worlds are trembling and exceedingly afraid; "I see"—this is the connection with the preceding verse. //20//
Madhusūdana says: He describes the pervasiveness of the form of the Blessed One under discussion with the words "dyāv-āpṛthivyoḥ.
Indeed, this space between heaven and earth—the intermediate region—is pervaded by You alone.
All directions are pervaded;

having seen this wondrous sight that causes extreme amazement, and having perceived this fierce form of yours which is difficult to grasp due to its great majesty, the three worlds have become deeply distressed and utterly terrified—
O Great-Souled One, O Giver of Fearlessness to the virtuous!
The intention is that from this point forward, one should summarize this [work]. //20//
Viśvanātha:
Now, because it is relevant to the context, he demonstrated that very form's nature as Time through ten verses beginning with "dyauḥ" (the sky). //20//
Baladeva said: Now, showing that this very form possesses the nature of time by virtue of its inherent utility, he says with ten verses beginning with "dyauḥ":
"The space between heaven and earth, as well as all the directions, are pervaded by You alone.
Having seen this immeasurable, wonderful, and formidable form of Yours, the three worlds are distressed, terrified, and trembling."
O Great-Souled One, O Refuge of All!

This is understood here: even those gods, asuras, gandharvas, kinnaras, and others dwelling in the three worlds who had assembled to witness the battle—whether friends or neutrals—though they were full of devotion and possessed divine eyes granted by the Blessed One, did not perceive that form.
This was done by Arjuna alone, as if with his own hands, for the sake of providing many witnesses to his own sovereignty over the chariots and other objects appearing in the dream. //20//
For these hosts of gods are entering into You;
some, overcome with fear, offer praise with palms joined in reverence.
Having uttered "Svasti," the hosts of great seers and perfected beings praise you with abundant hymns of praise. //21//
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the words "amī hi":
these hosts of gods, being terrified, enter you—that is, they take refuge in you.
Among them, some who are exceedingly afraid remain at a distance with their two hands joined in the *añjali* gesture, and uttering "Victory! Victory! Protect! Protect!", they offer their prayers.
The rest is clear. //21//
Madhusūdana:
Seeing the Blessed Lord manifesting His own role in removing the burden of the earth, he says, "These," and so forth.

Indeed, these hosts of gods—the groups of deities such as the Vasus and others—having descended in human form for the purpose of relieving the earth's burden, are seen entering You while engaged in battle. They are perceived as entering You.
Likewise, by breaking down the phrase "evam asura-saṅghāḥ," it should also be understood that Duryodhana and others, who have become a burden to the earth, enter into You.
Thus, from both armies, some who are terrified yet unable even to flee, praise and extol You with palms joined in reverence.
When the battle has thus commenced, having observed omens such as portents, [they pray]: "May there be well-being for the entire world."

Having spoken thus, the hosts of great sages and Siddhas, headed by Nārada and others who had come to witness the battle, praise you with abundant words—speeches that convey the excellence of your qualities—in order to avert the destruction of the universe. //21//
Viśvanātha: [He addresses] you, "tvā. //21//
Baladeva: These hosts of gods are entering into You for refuge.
Among them, some, being terrified, stand at a distance with palms joined in reverence and cry out, "Save us! Save us, O Lord!"—thus they pray.
Perceiving this great fear, the assemblies of great sages and the hosts of perfected beings (siddhas), having uttered "May there be well-being for the universe," offer hymns of praise. 21.
The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and those who are the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, the Maruts, and the Uṣmapās;
The hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Siddhas all gaze upon you, filled with wonder. //22//
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and Rudra":
the Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and those who are the Sādhyas—these are the hosts beginning with Rudra.
The Viśvedevas; the Aśvins;
and the two gods, the Aśvins.
And the Maruts are the winds;
and the ancestors are the drinkers of heat,
for according to the Vedic revelation, "the ancestors indeed have heat as their portion."
And according to tradition, those who observe silence eat as long as the food remains warm;
the ancestors eat as long as the qualities of the sacrificial offering have not been described.
Thus:
the Gandharvas, the Yakṣas, and the Asuras such as Virocana,
and the hosts of Siddhas, which are the assemblies of the Siddhas.
The grammatical connection is: "All of them, being struck with wonder, were gazing at you. //22//
Madhusūdana:
Furthermore, regarding the word "Rudra":
the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Vasus, and those divine hosts named Sādhyas are all included by the two terms *viśvedeva*, which possess the same grammatical case-ending.
O Lord, while being addressed, the hosts of gods— the Aśvins, the Nāsatyas, the Damras, the forty-nine Maruts,
the Uṣmapās, the Pitṛs, and the multitudes and assemblies of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Siddhas— all behold you;
because of such a wondrous sight, they are all struck with amazement and a sense of extraordinary, supermundane wonder.
And they fall into [them]. //22//
Viśvanātha:
They are called *uṣmapāḥ* (the steam-drinkers), meaning the ancestors who drink the steam;
for the Śruti states, "The ancestors indeed have steam as their portion. //22//
Baladeva: It is clear that "Rudra" refers to this.
According to the Nirukta, the ancestors (pitaraḥ) are "steam-drinkers" (uṣmapāḥ), meaning they drink steam;
and according to the Śruti, "the ancestors indeed have steam as their portion. //22//
O mighty-armed one, this great form of yours has many mouths and eyes, and many arms, thighs, and feet.
Seeing that many-bellied form, terrible with many fangs, the worlds were struck with terror, as was I.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, as for the form—O mighty-armed one, having seen your great and exceedingly powerful form, all the worlds are deeply distressed and terrified;
likewise, I too am deeply distressed.
Having seen what kind of form? That which possesses many mouths and eyes; that which possesses many arms, thighs, and feet.
That which has many bellies;
that which is formidable and distorted by many fangs—meaning, it is fierce. //23//
Madhusūdana concludes what was said regarding the three worlds being greatly distressed with the words "the form":
O mighty-armed one, having seen your form, all the worlds— all living beings— have become greatly distressed, and likewise I am distressed by fear.
What is your form like?
It is great and of immense proportions;
it is that which possesses many mouths and eyes.

The meaning is: having seen that [form] which has many arms, thighs, and feet; which has many bellies; and which is formidable and exceedingly terrifying with its many fangs, all the worlds, together with me, were afflicted by fear as soon as they saw it. //23//
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: He concludes what was stated—that the three worlds were greatly distressed—with the words "a vast form.
It was formidable and fierce, with many fangs.
The rest is clear;
thus, "I" is to be connected with what follows. //23//
Touching the sky, blazing, multicolored, with wide-gaping mouths and glowing, vast eyes.
For upon seeing you, O Viṣṇu, my inner self is deeply distressed; I find neither fortitude nor peace.
Śrīdhara: It is not merely that "I am afraid";
rather, [he says] "touching the sky.
That which touches the sky (*nabhas*) is *nabhaḥ-spṛk*; the meaning is that it pervades the intermediate space (*antarīkṣa*).
Blazing, endowed with splendor;
having many colors;
having faces that are manifest and wide-open.
I am one whose inner self and mind are deeply distressed upon seeing you thus—with eyes that are blazing and wide—and therefore I find no steadfastness, courage, or tranquility. 24.
Madhusūdana elaborates on this very terror with the words "The sky...
and so forth: it is not only that I am distressed upon seeing you, but my inner self—that is, my mind—is also deeply agitated.

Thus, O Viṣṇu, I find— that is, I do not obtain— *dhṛti*, which is fortitude or the capacity to sustain the body, senses, and so forth, nor *śama*, which is tranquility of mind; for what kind of You am I [to know]?
Having seen you— touching the heavens, pervading the intermediate space,
blazing, aflame, possessing many colors, endowed with various terrifying forms, with gaping mouth, wide-open face,
and glowing, vast eyes— I am deeply distressed in my inner self.
The grammatical connection is: "I find neither fortitude nor tranquility. //24//
Viśvanātha:
*Śama* means tranquility (*upaśama*). //24//
Baladeva: Manifesting a sense of humility intended to bring about the withdrawal of this form, he says in two verses beginning with "nabhaḥ-spṛśam":
"O Viṣṇu! Having seen You, my inner self is deeply distressed; with a mind terrified and agitated, I find neither fortitude nor peace."
Of what kind? "Touching the sky," meaning pervading the atmosphere; "with gaping mouth," meaning with a wide-open mouth.
The rest is clear in its meaning.
Here, the sentiment of terror (*bhayānaka-rasa*) is expressed by himself, caused by the perception of his form as Time (*kāla*). //24//
And having seen Your mouths, terrible with tusks and resembling the fire of cosmic destruction, BhG 11.25.
I do not know the directions, nor do I find peace; be gracious, O Lord of Gods, O Abode of the World! //25//
Śrīdhara: Regarding the word "daṃṣṭra" (fang):
O Lord of Gods, having seen your faces, I do not know the directions due to the onset of fear, nor do I obtain *śarma*, which is happiness.
O Abode of the World, be gracious!
Having seen what kind of faces?
Terrifying with tusks; "Kālānala" refers to the fire of universal destruction due to its distorted nature.
Those which are similar to that. //25//
Madhusūdana:

Merely upon seeing your mouths—which are formidable with fangs, terrifying due to their distorted shapes, and resembling the fire at the time of universal dissolution—I do not know the directions, such as east and west, because I am overcome by fear. I do not know them even by distinguishing between them.
Therefore, I find no peace or happiness even upon beholding Your form.
Hence, O Lord of Gods, O Abode of the Universe, be gracious; be well-disposed toward me. The implication is: "so that, by Your continued presence, I may obtain the bliss born of seeing You. (25)
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: "With fangs" (daṃṣṭra);
"like the fire of time" (kālānala) means like the fire of universal dissolution (pralayāgni), resembling or equal to it.
Śarma means happiness. //25//
And here are all these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with the hosts of earthly rulers, [beholding] you.
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and that son of a Sūta, together with our own foremost warriors as well. //26//
Hurrying, they enter your mouths,
which are terrifying and formidable with tusks;
some are caught between the teeth.
They are seen with their heads crushed to pieces. //27//

Śrīdhara: Regarding what the Blessed One said—"And whatever else you wish to see, look at it here in my body, including the future victory or defeat in this battle"—now, looking [at that], he says "These" and so forth in five verses. "These" refers to all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, beginning with Duryodhana.
Together with the multitudes—that is, the assemblies—of kings such as Jayadratha and others, [the warriors] enter your mouths; this is the connection with the following verse.
Likewise, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and that son of a Sūta, Karṇa.
Not only they alone enter [the battle], but also our opposing combatants—those chief warriors such as Śikhaṇḍin, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and others—together with them. //26//

"Those who are all these [beings] running in haste toward your gaping mouths—mouths that are jagged, deformed, and terrifying—they enter them; and among them, some are seen caught between the gaps of the teeth, distinguished by their heads being ground to powder. //27//
Madhusūdana said:

"O Guḍākeśa, it is my constant desire to see our victory and the defeat of the enemies; behold now within my body whatever else you wish to see. Thus commanded by the Blessed One, Arjuna says with these five verses, beginning with "Behold," that he is now seeing [the vision].

And these hundred brothers of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Duryodhana and the others, with the exception of Yuyutsu, are all entering you in haste; this is the connection with the preceding verse. Here, the deficiency of the verbal action [the verb "enter" being understood] is actually a merit, as it serves to indicate extreme fear. Together with the hosts of kings, such as the Ādīnas, they are indeed entering you.

The connection is as follows: not only do Duryodhana and the others enter, but even Bhīṣma—who was esteemed by all as invincible—Droṇa, Karṇa the son of a Sūta, and that one who has always been my enemy, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and other such preeminent warriors among our own men as if they were enemies, are entering You. //26//
All these, beginning with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, are entering your terrifying mouths, which are formidable with tusks, in great haste.
And therein, some with their heads crushed, are seen by me clearly and without doubt to be caught and firmly stuck between your teeth. (27)
Viśvanātha: Nothing.

Baladeva: With the words "And whatever else you wish to see," the Blessed One stated that one should behold the future victory, defeat, and so forth of this battle within His own body; now, beholding that, [Arjuna] speaks with these five verses beginning with "And these... (amī ca).

These sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Duryodhana and the others, along with all the hosts of kings—Śalya, Jayadratha, and the multitude of other monarchs—are entering his mouths in haste; this is the connection with what follows. And those who were renowned for their invincibility, Bhīṣma and the rest, they too [enter].
The word "asau" (this one) means that he is always my enemy;
it refers to Karṇa, the son of a charioteer.

It is not only they [the Kauravas], but also our own chief warriors such as Dhṛṣṭadyumna and others who enter along with them—this use of the term "together" (*saha*) constitutes the poetic figure *sahokti*.
"Among them, some—with their heads crushed—were seen by me stuck between the teeth, at the junctions of the fangs. (26–27)
Just as the many currents of water in rivers flow directly toward the ocean, so do these [beings] come to me.
In this same way, these heroes of the world of men enter your blazing mouths. //28//
Śrīdhara: He explains the very entry by means of an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as).
Just as the many currents of water—the flows of the waters of rivers that have set out upon various paths—move toward and enter the ocean alone;
even so, these heroes of the world of men enter, and likewise these people also enter your mouths. //28//
Madhusūdana says:
He provides an illustration regarding the entry [of kings] into the mouth of the Blessed One with the words "just as" (yathā).
Just as there are many swift currents—many rapid flows—of waters belonging to rivers that proceed along many paths.

Just as rivers, facing the ocean, run and enter only the ocean, so do these heroes of the world of men enter your mouths, which blaze on all sides—or rather, according to another reading, "blaze forth intensely. //28//
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: He states two examples regarding entry with the words "yathā" (as) in two verses.
Of these, the first concerns entry preceded by study (*adhyayana*).
But the second [type of killing] is to be understood as occurring when preceded by conscious intent. //28//
Just as moths with full force enter a blazing fire for their destruction, so do they enter me.
In that very same way, the worlds, with their full momentum, enter your mouths for destruction. //29//
Śrīdhara: Regarding entry by way of lack of control, the force of a river's current was cited as an illustration.
He states an illustration for entry preceded by conscious intent with the word "yathā" (just as):
just as moths, that is, locusts, whose speed is increased by conscious intent, enter a blazing fire for destruction—that is, for death alone—so too do these people.
They enter into your mouths. //29//
Madhusūdana says:
Having stated the illustration of the river's current for entering without prior reflection, he states the illustration for entering with prior reflection, beginning with "yathā" (just as):
just as moths, that is, locusts, possessing great speed, enter a blazing fire intentionally.
For their destruction and for death, even so, all these worlds—Duryodhana and the others—enter your mouths with full force, intentionally and without regard for the future. (29)
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: Jvalana means fire (vahni). //29//
Devouring all the worlds on every side with your flaming mouths, you lick them up.
O Viṣṇu, having filled the entire world with your splendors, your fierce radiances blaze forth. //30//
Śrīdhara: Then, what [happens] on all sides? To this he says: "lelihyase" (you lick), meaning you swallow and gulp down.
You lick— that is, you consume excessively— all these heroes, all these worlds, from every side and in every way.
By what? By blazing mouths.
Furthermore, O Viṣṇu, your rays—your splendors and flashes of light—having pervaded the entire world with their brilliance, they fiercely and truly scorch and torment it. //30//

Madhusūdana, having described the manner in which the kings desirous of fighting enter the mouth of the Blessed One, now speaks of the manner in which the Blessed One and His effulgence then proceed, saying: "Le-li-hya-se" (He is licking).
Thus, swallowing all those people, Duryodhana and the others, who were entering with such speed, He was drawing them into His interior.

With your blazing faces, you lick and taste from all sides and everywhere; having filled the entire world with your splendors and radiance, because you fill the world with radiance, therefore your fierce and intense rays, like those of a burning fire, scorch and produce heat.
O Viṣṇu, whose nature is all-pervading! //30//
Viśvanātha: [Nothing].
Baladeva: Having described the manner in which the warriors enter His mouth, He speaks of the manner in which His splendors proceed there with the words *lelihāse* ("You lick...").

As all the worlds, including Duryodhana and the others, enter with speed, You swallow them with Your flaming mouths; and out of an intense onset of wrath, You lick on all sides Your lips and other parts, which are smeared with their blood.
O Viṣṇu, your fierce splendors and radiances gaze upon me again and again, scorching the entire world by filling it with unbearable energies.
"O Pervader of the Universe!
It is impossible to flee from you"—this is the meaning. //30//
Tell me who you are, O one of fierce form;
salutations be unto you, O best of gods, be gracious!
I desire to know you, the Primordial One;
for I do not understand your activity. //31//
Śrīdhara: Since this is so, therefore say:
"Who are you of fierce form? Tell me, tell me; speak!"
Homage be to you!
O best of gods, be gracious; be well-disposed.
I desire to know you, the primordial Person, in detail.
Since I do not know your activity or your effort—that is, for what purpose you have thus engaged—I do not even know the news of your activity as one who has become such as this. //31//
Madhusūdana said: "Since this is so, therefore tell me:
who are you, possessing such a fierce form and cruel appearance? Tell me, for I am one who is most worthy of your favor."
Therefore, let there be salutation to you, the teacher of all; O best of gods, be gracious—grant me your favor by relinquishing your cruelty.
I desire to know specifically, to understand you, the primordial one and the cause of all; for even though I am your friend, I do not comprehend your activity or your purpose. //31//
Viśvanātha: Nothing.

Baladeva: Having thus described the Blessed One in His universal form (*viśva-rūpa*), in which the power of time (*kāla-śakti*) is manifested, Arjuna—though he already knows that reality—asks, "Tell me," in order to strengthen his own understanding. When the Blessed One, having been requested by him to "show me Your imperishable Self," displayed that divine form characterized by a thousand heads and so forth, He further revealed His exceedingly terrible nature as the Destroyer.
It is being demonstrated:
"In this regard, tell me, declare who you are, you of fierce form;
O best of gods!"
Let there be homage to you!
Be gracious and abandon this fierce form;
I especially desire to know you, the Primordial One.
"I do not indeed know your activity or your exertion; tell me the purpose for which you have thus engaged yourself. //31//
The Blessed Lord said:
I am Time, the destroyer of worlds, now come forth.
Engaged here in the destruction of the worlds,
even without you all these warriors stationed in the opposing armies shall cease to exist.
Śrīdhara: Being thus entreated, the Blessed One spoke in three verses beginning with "I am Time.
I am Time, the increaser, exceedingly fierce, the destroyer of worlds;
I have set out here in this world to withdraw all living beings from the worlds.
Therefore, even without you—the slayer—even in your absence, they shall not exist; they shall not live.
Although these are not to be slain by you, nevertheless, being seized by me in the form of Time (Kāla), they will surely die.
Who are they? Those who are in the opposing armies—armies against armies.
All those warriors who were stationed in all the armies of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the others as well; //32//
Madhusūdana:
Thus requested by Arjuna, He [the Lord] explains in three verses everything for whose sake He Himself acts—that is, "I am Time" (*kālo 'smi*).
I am now Time, the Supreme Lord endowed with the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), the destroyer of all; I have now become fully grown, having reached my full development.
Listen to the purpose for which I have set out: at this time, I have begun to withdraw and consume the worlds.
If you ask, "How could this be so without my activity?"—the answer is no;
for even without you, O Arjuna, even without you as a warrior, and even without your intervention, it would happen through my activity alone.

All those who are considered unworthy of fighting— Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, and others— as well as whatever other warriors are stationed in the opposing ranks, the enemy armies, shall cease to exist simply because they have been slain by me.
The meaning is that, in that case, your activity is of no avail. //32//
Viśvanātha: Nothing. Baladeva: Being thus entreated, the Blessed One said, "I am Time," meaning he has grown great and is all-pervading.

The meaning is that "I am that Time" who is proclaimed by the Śruti: "He for whom both Brahminhood and Kshatriyahood are the rice, and for whom death is the condiment—who truly knows where He is? (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.25).
Know that at this time I have begun to gather in—that is, to swallow up—the worlds, Duryodhana and the others, as well as the fruit of my own activity.
Except for you and Yudhiṣṭhira and the rest, all shall cease to exist; they shall not live.
Or rather, if it be asked, "How can their destruction occur if I withdraw from battle? he says in response: "even without [me]."

"Even without you as their warrior—that is, even without your participation in the battle—all of them will cease to exist; they will surely die, for I, in the form of Time, shall take away their life-span.
Who are all these? He says: those who stand in the opposing ranks, Bhīṣma and the others, in both armies.
But for you, having withdrawn from battle, there would only be a fall from your own duty. //32//
Therefore, arise; win glory; having conquered your enemies, enjoy a prosperous kingdom.
"These have already been slain by me alone;
you, O Savyasācin, be merely the instrument."
Śrīdhara: "Therefore" means:
because this is so, therefore you arise for battle;
obtain—that is, attain—such fame as that Bhīṣma and the others, who were invincible even to the gods, have been conquered by Arjuna.
Having conquered your enemies without effort, enjoy a prosperous kingdom.
These enemies of yours have already been rendered as good as dead by me alone in the form of Time, even before your battle;
nevertheless, you remain merely the instrumental cause.

He is Savyasācin; by the etymology "one whose nature it is to draw (sācituṃ) and fix arrows with the left hand (savyena)," he is called Savyasācin because he can discharge arrows even with his left hand. //33//
Madhusūdana says: "Because it is so, therefore...
That is to say, since these [beings] will surely perish even without your intervention, you should therefore arise and exert yourself.
Go forth to battle and obtain such fame as this: that even Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and other great car-warriors (atiratha), who were difficult even for the gods to conquer, were swiftly defeated by Arjuna.
For it is only through great merits that fame is obtained.

Having conquered your enemies, Duryodhana and the others, without effort, enjoy the kingdom—make it your own possession and bring this prosperous, thornless realm to fruition. These enemies of yours were slain by me alone in the form of Time; their lifespans were already exhausted, and they were merely not struck down from their chariots before your battle so that you might obtain glory. Therefore, you are merely the instrumental cause, serving as the object of universal renown for the statement that "these were conquered by Arjuna."

O Savyasācin—one whose nature it is to collect (sacitum) and fix arrows even with the left hand (savyena)—the victory over Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and others is not impossible for you; therefore, the intention is that after your intervention, when these [opponents] are struck down from their chariots by me, people will attribute the agency to you alone. //33//
Viśvanātha: Nothing.

Baladeva: Since this is so, therefore you arise for your own duty, for battle; win glory—attain that rare fame that Bhīṣma and the others, who were difficult even for the gods to conquer, have been vanquished by Arjuna with ease alone.

Previously, at the very time of the offense against Draupadī, these were slain by me for the sake of your fame; they merely function like mechanical puppets. Therefore, O Savyasācin, be a mere instrument.
The meaning is: "O showerer of arrows with both hands," referring to one whose nature it is to collect and fix arrows even with the left hand when a battle-intense situation has arrived. //33//
Drona and Bhishma, Jayadratha and Karna, as well as other heroic warriors.
Slay those already slain by me; do not be distressed.
Fight, and you shall conquer your enemies in battle. //34//
Śrīdhara: Nor should one entertain the doubt, "We do not know which of these two is better for us—whether we shall conquer them or they shall conquer us"; to this he says, "Droṇa," etc.
You should slay—that is, cause to be slain—those Droṇa and others from whom you fear;
do not be distressed, do not give way to fear.
You will certainly conquer—indeed, you shall defeat—your rivals and enemies in battle, in the fray. //34//
Madhusūdana said:
"But Droṇa is the best of Brahmins, a teacher of the science of archery, and specifically my own preceptor, endowed as he is with divine weapons;
likewise Bhīṣma, who possesses the power to choose the time of his own death and is endowed with divine weapons, has engaged in single combat with Paraśurāma."

Even when approached, he was not defeated; for his father, the aged Kṣatriya, performs penance with this vow: "The head of whoever shall cause my son’s head to fall upon the earth shall itself fall to the ground at that very moment. Thus Jayadratha is also impossible to conquer, as he himself is devoted to the propitiation of Mahādeva and is endowed with divine weapons, as is Karṇa.

Moreover, he himself is like the sun; through his worship of him, he has become endowed with divine weapons and distinguished by the *śakti*—the "man-slayer" granted by Vāsava—which cannot be rendered futile. Furthermore, there are great-souled men such as Kṛpa, Aśvatthāman, and Bhūriśravas, who are altogether invincible. While these remain, how shall I conquer my enemies and enjoy the kingdom? How?
To remove Arjuna’s apprehension that he might fail to attain glory, [the Lord] speaks, naming those who are the objects of that apprehension, beginning with "Droṇa":
"Slay all these heroic warriors, such as Droṇa and the rest— who have become the objects of your apprehension— already slain by Me in the form of Time."
What effort is there in slaying those who are already slain?
Therefore, do not be distressed; do not fall into the pain of agitation caused by fear, thinking, "How shall I be able to do this? Abandoning fear, fight!
You shall conquer—you will surely win—all your rivals, even all your enemies, in battle, in the conflict, before long.
Here, by the three occurrences of the word *ca* in "Droṇa, Bhīṣma, and Jayadratha," the previously mentioned doubt regarding invincibility is restated;
likewise, the word *tathā* refers to Karṇa as well,
and the word *api* in "and other heroic warriors" refers to them too.
Therefore, the intended meaning is: "Do not fear defeat from anyone, nor the sin resulting from their slaughter.

Just as in the verse, "How shall I fight against Bhīṣma and Droṇa in battle with arrows, O Madhusūdana, who are worthy of worship?"—where the connection with the individual members must be understood prior to the connection with the whole group—so too should it be seen here. (34)
Viśvanātha: [Silence].
Baladeva: With the intention that you have entertained doubt regarding your own victory—thinking, "Whether we shall conquer, or whether they shall conquer us"—he says, "And Drona," etc.
Slay, that is, kill, Drona and the others, whose lives have been taken by me.
"Do not hesitate;
do not fall into fear, thinking, 'How can I alone defeat these who are endowed with divine weapons?
The meaning is: what effort is there in killing those who are already dead?"
Abandoning fear, fight; you shall conquer, you will be victorious over the enemies who oppose you in battle. //34//
BhG 11.35 Sañjaya said:
Having heard these words of Keśava,
With palms joined in reverence, trembling, and bowing down again and again, the diadem-wearing Arjuna, overcome with fear, spoke to Kṛṣṇa with a faltering voice. //35//
