Śrīdhara: Then, regarding what occurred thereafter, Sañjaya spoke to Dhṛtarāṣṭra as follows:

"Having heard these words of Keśava—consisting of the three preceding verses—the diadem-wearer Arjuna, trembling and quivering, with palms joined in reverence (*kṛtāñjali*), bowed to Kṛṣṇa and spoke again."
How did he speak? "With a faltering voice" means that which is accompanied by a trembling of the throat due to the onset of joy, fear, and so forth; it was spoken in such a manner.
Furthermore, being even more afraid than one who is already afraid, he bowed down, having become prostrate. //35//
Madhusūdana:
Once Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Jayadratha, and Karṇa—the objects of hope for victory—have been slain, Duryodhana will be as good as dead when left without support.
Realizing this, if Dhṛtarāṣṭra should abandon his hope for victory and make peace, then there would be tranquility.
Intending that this might happen for both sides, and then, in response to the expectation of what occurred next, Sañjaya said:

"This. Having heard these previously mentioned words of Keśava, Arjuna—the one to whom Indra gave the crown (Kirīṭin), who is renowned for his supreme heroism, and who was trembling with agitation born from seeing the supreme wonder—spoke to Kṛṣṇa with palms joined in reverence.
Having bowed down again and again to the Blessed One, who removes the sins of His devotees, he spoke once more with a faltering voice;

"with a faltering voice" (*sa-gadgada*) means that while his eyes were filled with tears due to fear and joy, his speech became slow and trembling because his throat was constricted by phlegm— describing him in such a state.
The connection of the words is as follows: being "bhītabhītaḥ," that is, extremely terrified, he first paid homage, and then having bowed again and become utterly humble, he spoke. //35//
Viśvanātha:
"Having paid homage" (*namaskṛtya*) is an archaic Vedic form (ārṣa). //35//
Baladeva: Then, regarding what occurred, Sañjaya said, "This," etc.

Having heard these three verses of Keśava’s speech, Kirīṭin Pārtha—trembling with agitation born from the sight of that most wonderful and most fierce form—bowed down; *namaskṛtya* is used here in the Vedic sense.
Having paid obeisance to Kṛṣṇa and bowing down again,
being terrified and overwhelmed with extreme fear, he spoke once more, with a faltering voice accompanied by a trembling throat. //35//
BhG 11.36 Arjuna said:
"It is fitting, O Hṛṣīkeśa, that by the proclamation of Your [glory]..."
The world rejoices and becomes devoted;
the rākṣasas, terrified, flee in all directions, and all the hosts of siddhas pay homage. //36//
Śrīdhara: "In the proper place"—this is Arjuna's speech consisting of eleven words.
*Sthāne* is an indeclinable used in the sense of "it is fitting.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, since you are thus of such wonderful power and affectionate toward your devotees.
Therefore, by your glorification— that is, by the proclamation of your majesty— not only do I alone rejoice,
but the entire world rejoices, attaining intense delight.
The meaning is that this is indeed appropriate and fitting.
Likewise, that the world is delighted and attains affection;
likewise, that the *rākṣasas*, being terrified,
flee and run away toward the various directions.

That all the assemblies of those perfected in yoga, austerity, mantras, and so forth, bow down to and pay homage [to him], is indeed appropriate and fitting; the meaning is that this is not surprising. //36//
Madhusūdana:
Arjuna spoke with eleven [verses]. "Sthāne" is an indeclinable used in the sense of "fittingly" (yuktam).
O Hṛṣīkeśa,
O director of all the senses! Since you possess such exceedingly wonderful power and are affectionate toward your devotees,
therefore, through the exalted glorification of you— that is, by the chanting and hearing of your praise which is beyond compare— [one attains peace].

And it is not only I who rejoice; rather, the meaning is that it is entirely appropriate and fitting that the whole world—every sentient being—rejoices, attaining supreme joy, because they oppose the Rākṣasa. Likewise, it is also entirely fitting that the whole world is filled with affection, developing a sense of endearment toward him.
Likewise, that the *rakṣas* beings, being terrified and overcome with fear, flee in all directions—that too is entirely fitting.
Similarly, that the entire assembly of perfected ones (*siddhas*), such as Kapila and others, pay homage—that too is entirely fitting.
In every instance, this connects with the words "because of your glorification" (*tava prakīrtyā*) and "in this place" (*sthāne*).
This verse is renowned in the treatises on mantras as a mantra for the destruction of Rākṣasas;
it should be understood that its secret lies in being encapsulated by the eight-syllable Nārāyaṇa mantra and the Sudarśana weapon mantra. //36//
Viśvanātha:

Having suddenly realized that this extreme graciousness and extreme ferocity of the Lord’s form concern those who are turned toward Him and those who are turned away from Him, he praises that very reality by saying "sthāne" (it is fitting).
The word *sthāne* is an indeclinable meaning "it is fitting. O Hṛṣīkeśa!
O You who direct the senses of Your devotees toward Yourself and toward Your own supremacy!

The meaning is this: by your preeminent glorification—that is, by the proclamation of your majesty—this world rejoices and becomes devoted; thus, it is entirely fitting that the world is oriented toward you. Likewise, it is also appropriate and logical that the *rakṣasas*—the *rakṣasas*, asuras, dānavas, piśācas, and so forth—becoming terrified, flee toward the various directions, running away from all sides.
The meaning is that this is because they are turned away from you.
Likewise, it is also entirely appropriate that the assemblies of all those who have attained perfection through devotion to you pay homage;
the meaning is that this is because they are devotees of you.
This verse is well known in the treatises on mantras as a mantra for the destruction of demons. //36//
Baladeva: Having observed simultaneously, like colors on a stage, both the extreme loveliness and the extreme ferocity of Kṛṣṇa— the friend of the Supreme Lord—
Arjuna, knowing that these two qualities pertain respectively to the object facing him and the object turned away from him, praises Him accordingly with eleven verses beginning with "sthāne."
The word *sthāne* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) ending in *-e*, having the sense of "it is fitting.
The address *he hṛṣīkeśa* refers to the state of being either "facing toward" or "turned away from" the senses; thus, the meaning is "O Supreme One.

The world—headed by gods, gandharvas, siddhas, and vidyādharas—who has come to witness the battle, rejoices and is filled with devotion toward You because of Your renown as the destroyer of the wicked. This world stands before You.
And this is logical:

it is also logical that the demons, Rākṣasas, Asuras, Dānavas, and others, who are evil by nature and averse to you, having become terrified by the proclamation of his praises sung forth by the gods and others, flee and run away in all directions.
The sense is that this is because You manifest forms in accordance with the nature of living beings.

Thus, seeing Your capacity to favor both the disciplined and the undisciplined, all the hosts of Siddhas, including Sanaka and the others, who are Your devotees, offer salutations and bow down while crying out, "Victory! Victory! O Blessed One! This is fitting, for You captivate the hearts of Your devotees.
And why, O Great-Souled One, should they not bow down to You, who are greater even than Brahmā, the original creator?
O infinite Lord of gods, abode of the universe, you are the imperishable, that which is both being and non-being, and that which is beyond them. //37//
Śrīdhara: He states the reason for that with the words "kasmāt" (from what?). O Great-Souled One! O Infinite One!
O Lord of Gods!
O Abode of the Universe!
For what reason would they not bow down to you, why would they not offer salutation?
To whom? To him who is more venerable (*garīyase*) than even Brahmā, the most weighty teacher;
and to the original creator (*ādi-kartre*), the progenitor even of Brahmā.
Furthermore, he is the imperishable Brahman, the fundamental cause (*mūla-kāraṇa*) which is beyond both the manifest (*sat-avyakta*) and the unmanifest (*asat-avyakta*).
And that is you yourself;
the meaning is that it is not surprising that everyone pays homage to you for these nine reasons. //37//
Madhusūdana [Śrīdhara] states the reason why the Blessed One is the object of joy and so forth with the words "And for what reason" (*kasmāc ca*).
And for what reason (*kasmāc ca hetoḥ*) would all the hosts of perfected beings (*siddha-saṅghāḥ*) not bow down to you, not offer salutation (*na nameran*)?
O Great-Souled One, O You of supremely noble mind; O Infinite One, O You who are empty of all conceptual limitations;
O Lord of Gods, O Ruler even of the gods beginning with Hiraṇyagarbha!
O Abode of the World, O Support of All!
To what kind of You—who are weightier than even Brahmā, being his most venerable teacher and primordial creator—to You who are the progenitor even of Brahmā [do I bow]?
Whether it be the quality of being a controller, a teacher, or a progenitor, each one of these reasons individually serves as a ground for Your being worthy of salutation.

Furthermore, the particle *ca* (and) has the sense of "why" (*kasmāt*) in the phrase "for what reason [is there] salutation? and serves to indicate that it is not surprising that he is "accumulated with various auspicious qualities," such as his great magnanimity, infinity, and being the abode of the world.
Moreover, what is it that exists? It exists as something perceived through the mode of affirmation (*vidhi-mukhena*).
That which is perceived through the mode of negation is "it does not exist.
Alternatively, you alone are both the manifest existent and the unmanifest non-existent;
likewise, you are that which is beyond them.

The meaning is that even that which is the supreme root cause, the imperishable Brahman, which transcends both those [categories] of existence and non-existence, is You alone; there is nothing whatsoever distinct from You.
Some read the word "ca" (also) before the word "yat" in the phrase "tat-param yat.
The meaning is that it is not at all surprising that everyone bows down to You for these reasons. //37//
Viśvanātha:
Why should they not bow?
On the contrary, they should indeed bow.
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used in the archaic style (*ārṣa*).
You are that Imperishable Brahman which is beyond both the effect, which is existent, and the cause, which is non-existent. //37//

Baladeva: Now, by means of four verses beginning with "And why?", [the Lord] establishes His state as the Self of all through His omnipresence, while declaring the Blessed One’s worthiness of universal homage.
O Great-Souled One, O Noble-Minded One!
O Infinite One, O Pervader of All!
O Lord of gods, controller of all gods;
O Abode of the world, refuge of all—
why would those hosts of perfected beings not bow down to you?
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is Vedic;
however, they would indeed bow down. To whom? He says: "To such a one."

Because there are many reasons for offering salutation to Him who is even weightier than Brahmā—more venerable to the primordial creator who brings about the creation of the principles (tattvas)—this constitutes the figure of speech known as *samuccaya* (accumulation). Furthermore, that which is the imperishable (*akṣara*) principle of *prakṛti*, and that which is beyond it: from that *jīvātman*-principle conjoined with *prakṛti*, and from the *prakṛti*-principle in the form described, You alone are the one who is supreme, most excellent, and distinct—the liberated *jīvātman*-principle, O You whose form is all things.
This is the meaning. //37//
You are the primordial God, the ancient Person;
you are the supreme repository of this universe.
You are the knower and the object of knowledge, and the supreme abode;
by you the entire universe is pervaded, O You of infinite forms. //38//
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, "You are the primordial God" (ādi-deva) means that You are the beginning of the gods;
for You are the ancient, beginningless Puruṣa.
Therefore, you are its supreme treasure-house and place of dissolution;
likewise, you are the knower of the universe. Furthermore, whatever collection of objects is to be known, and even that supreme abode, the station of Viṣṇu—that too is you alone.
Therefore, O You of infinite forms, this entire universe has been pervaded by You alone;
and by these seven reasons, the meaning is that You alone are the one to be saluted. //38//
Madhusūdana:
Out of an excess of devotion, he praises [the Lord] once more with the word "thou" (*tvam*).
Thou art the primordial god (*ādi-deva*) because of being the cause of the creation of the world.
The Puruṣa is the fulfiller;
he is the ancient, beginningless one.
You are the supreme repository of this universe, for it is the place of dissolution; everything is deposited within you.

Having thus described [the Self] as the material cause by virtue of being the locus of creation, dissolution, and persistence, He declares its status as the efficient cause while distinguishing it from *pradhāna* (primordial matter) through its omniscience: "You are the knower, the perceiver of all. He wards off the implication of duality by stating: "And that which is to be known (*vedya*), You alone are that too," because all objects of knowledge are merely conceptual constructs (*kalpita*) due to the absence of any ultimate relationship with the perceiver, whose nature is pure consciousness. For this very reason: "And that which is the supreme abode—the dense mass of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, free from ignorance and its effects, the highest step of Viṣṇu—that too is You alone."

O You of infinite and undivided nature, this entire universe—the effect which is devoid of its own existence and manifestation—is pervaded by You, the cause, who exist as both the real form (*sad-rūpa*) and the manifesting consciousness (*sphuraṇa-rūpa*), through a relationship that is purely illusory (*māyika*) during the period of its persistence. //38//
Viśvanātha:
The treasure-house is the place of dissolution, the supreme abode, the essential nature that transcends the qualities (guṇas). //38//
Baladeva says: "Thou" (tvam).

The supreme treasure, the ultimate refuge—according to etymology (*nirukti*), that in which everything is deposited. He who is the knower in the world and that which is to be known—both of these are Thou alone.
If it is asked, "Why is this so?", he says in response: "Because this entire universe is pervaded by you"—this is the meaning.

Furthermore, that supreme abode known as the Supreme Void (*paramavyoman*), the place to be attained, is also you alone, because that abode is the manifestation of the power called *Parā* which is you. (38)
You are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, Śaśāṅka, Prajāpati, and the Great-Grandfather.
Homage, homage be to you a thousand times;
and yet again, further still, homage, homage to you! //39//
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, praising you as one who alone is to be saluted by all because you are the self of all the gods, he himself also offers salutation with the words "Vāyu," etc.
The statement that you are in the form of Vāyu and so forth is intended to illustrate your nature as the self of all the gods.
You are Prajāpati, the Grandfather.
Since you are also his progenitor, you are his great-grandfather;
therefore, let there be salutation to you a thousandfold,
and again, let there be salutation a thousand times.
Furthermore, yet again, a thousand times over, "Homage! Homage! //39//
Madhusūdana:
Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, and Śaśāṅka—this is also an elliptical expression for Sūrya and the others;
as well as Prajāpati, Virāṭ, and Hiraṇyagarbha.
You are the great-grandfather of the Grandfather Hiraṇyagarbha, and you are even his father.
Since you are thus the self of all the gods, you alone are to be saluted by everyone; therefore, let there be obeisance, obeisance, obeisance to you from me, a wretched man, a thousand times over.
And again, yet again, and once more—obeisance, obeisance to you!
The absence of any sense of "enough" regarding prostrations due to an excess of devotion and faith is indicated by this repetition of prostrations. //39//

Viśvanātha: Nothing. Baladeva: Therefore, he says "Vāyu" to show that you are the referent of the word "all. You are the one who represents all the gods, appearing in the forms of all the gods beginning with Vāyu; you are Prajāpati, the four-faced Grandfather.

Because You are their father, You are their great-grandfather, just as gold is in relation to bracelets and other ornaments; since You, the Cause who possesses the powers of both consciousness and matter, pervade the air and all else, You are the embodiment of all those various forms. Therefore, saying "I bow to You," he says: "Salutation after salutation. (39)
Salutations to You from the front and from behind;
let there be salutations to You from every side, O All.
You possess infinite vigor and immeasurable prowess;
you pervade all things, and therefore you are everything. //40//

Śrīdhara: Not attaining satiety in his prostrations due to an excess of devotion, faith, and fear, he bows again and again, saying "namaḥ. O All, O Soul of All, let there be salutation to You in all directions.
Establishing that You are the soul of all, he says: "whose power and capacity are infinite (ananta-vīrya)."
He whose valor (*vikrama*) and prowess (*parākrama*) are immeasurable—being such as this, You completely pervade and encompass the entire universe both internally and externally.
Just as gold exists by pervading its own effects such as bracelets and earrings, You abide having pervaded [all things]; therefore, You are the essential nature of all. //40//
Madhusūdana: "Salutation be to you in front," that is, in the foremost part; or rather, "let there be salutation to you in front.
The word *atha* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*).
Homage should be paid to you even from behind;
let there be homage to you, O All, who are situated in every direction and in all respects.
"Vīrya" is physical strength, "vikrama" is prowess, and "śikṣā" is skill in the application of weapons.

It has been said, "I consider one to be superior in valor and another to be superior in training," whereby Bhīma, Duryodhana, and each of the others were established as distinct. But you, being both of infinite power and immeasurable prowess, constitute a single complete entity. Or, "O Anantavīrya" may be taken as a vocative address.

You pervade the entire world completely; you reach it through your single true form and, as the Self of all, you extend throughout it. Therefore, you are everything; the meaning is that there is nothing whatsoever apart from you.
Viśvanātha [comments]:
You pervade—that is, you extend through—your own effect, the world, just as gold pervades bracelets, earrings, and so forth; therefore, you alone are everything. (40)
Baladeva, finding himself unable to contain his overflowing devotion through mere prostrations, bows down many times, saying, "Salutation in front.
O All-pervading One! Let there be salutation after salutation to You who abide in front, behind, and on every side.
*Ananta* is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
"Vigor" (*vīrya*) is physical strength, whereas "valor" (*vikrama*) is the power of the intellect, consisting of proficiency in the employment of weapons and so forth;
for it was said with reference to Bhīma and Duryodhana: "One considers one [Bhīma] superior in vigor, and the other [Duryodhana] superior in training."
Regarding its being of all forms, he says: "You pervade everything. Thus it is stated in the Śrī-Vaiṣṇava:
"O Lord, this host of deities who has come into Your presence..."
"You alone are the creator of the world, since you are omnipresent. //40//
Thinking "he is my friend," whatever was said rashly—
addressing him as "O Kṛṣṇa," "O Yādava," or "O friend"— [for that I seek forgiveness].
Not knowing this greatness of yours, whether out of negligence or even out of affection, [I have acted thus]. //41//
And whatever disrespect you have suffered for the sake of mockery regarding dwellings, beds, seats, or food—
whether alone or even in their presence, O Acyuta;
Therefore, I beg forgiveness from you, the immeasurable one. //42//
Śrīdhara: Now, with two verses beginning with "sakhe," he asks the Blessed One for forgiveness.

The connection with the following verse is as follows: "Thinking that you are merely my friend in the worldly sense, whatever was said by me through force—that is, by way of insult—I beg forgiveness from you.
What was that? [The address: "O Kṛṣṇa! O Yādava! O friend! etc.
The hiatus (*sandhi*) is an archaic Vedic usage (*ārṣa*).

The reason for speaking with such force is as follows: "Whatever was spoken by me out of negligence or out of affection—that is, out of love—because I did not know of your majesty and this universal form. //41//
Furthermore, as for the phrase "and whatever":
O Acyuta, and whatever you have been treated with contempt during jests, sports, and the like; [for all that, I seek refuge].
"In one place" means alone;
that is, standing in private without her friends. Alternatively, "in their presence" means even before those laughing friends.
I beg forgiveness for all that multitude of offenses from you, who are immeasurable and of inconceivable power; I entreat you to grant me pardon. //42//
Madhusūdana says:

"Because I have incessantly committed offenses through my ignorance of your majesty, I now bow down to you, who are supremely compassionate, and ask for forgiveness for those offenses," he says in two verses beginning with "sakhe" (O friend).

Thinking, "You are my friend, being of equal age," whatever was said by me through an overbearing display of self-exaltation—namely, this universal form of yours (*viśvarūpa*) as well as your greatness and your extraordinary sovereignty (*aiśvaryātiśaya*)—[for that I seek your pardon].
"By me unknowingly"—that is, by me who was unaware of this majesty consisting of the universal form;
"out of negligence," meaning due to distraction of mind, or "even out of affection," meaning out of love—what was said? He says: "O Kṛṣṇa! O Yādava! O friend! (41)

And that which is done for the sake of derision or jest—whether it be in the monastery, in sleeping, sitting, or eating; where "monastery" refers to play or exercise; "sleeping" refers to specific types of bedding such as mattresses of cotton wool and the like;
and "sitting" refers to lion-thrones and so forth.

While many were eating, you ate from the mud among those objects [of desire]; you were treated with disrespect and insulted by them— whether you stood alone, having left your friends, in a secluded place,
or even in their presence,
O Acyuta, forever changeless one.
I beg forgiveness for all those faults consisting of verbal expressions and acts of disrespect; I implore you to forgive me.

The meaning is that my offenses, committed by one ignorant of your majesty, should be forgiven by the Blessed One, who is immeasurable, possessed of inconceivable power, changeless, and supremely compassionate. //42//
Viśvanātha:

"Alas, alas! Possessing such great and supreme sovereignty as this, yet I am one who has committed a multitude of great offenses against you"—thus, manifesting his remorse, he says, "O friend," meaning "O Kṛṣṇa."
You, Kṛṣṇa, are the son of a man named Vasudeva who is not even renowned as a half-charioteer;
O Yādava,
you possess no kingship over the lineage of Yadu.
"But for me, belonging to the lineage of Puru, there certainly exists kingship. "O friend!"—
this [sandhi] is an archaic (ārṣa) usage.
Furthermore, regarding that friendship of mine with you, neither your paternal influence nor your family lineage is the cause; rather, it is yours alone—this is the intended meaning.
With this in mind, I ask for forgiveness for what was said by me so forcefully and with contempt; "I forgive" connects with the subsequent clause.

This very form of yours, which consists of the universal form (*viśvarūpa*), is your own majesty; yet, out of negligence, or through affection and love, you have been treated with disrespect during sports and other pastimes for the sake of jest. You have been insulted with indirect speech such as "you are a speaker of truth," "you are guileless," and "you are supremely simple"—though you are indeed alone [in your nature].
Whether in private without my friends,
or even in their presence— when you stood before those joking friends, then all that occurred, that entire multitude of offenses, I beg forgiveness for,
O Lord!
"Forgive me" means "I entreat you. //41-42//

Baladeva: Thus Arjuna, having beheld his friend Kṛṣṇa characterized by a thousand heads and other such marks, and having praised and prostrated before him, addresses him with two verses beginning with "sakhe" (O friend), offering conciliation appropriate to that [vision], because his knowledge of his friend’s sovereignty was now intermingled [with direct perception].
Thinking and concluding, "Kṛṣṇa, the Blessed Lord, is my friend and companion," [Arjuna speaks of] this form of Yours characterized by a thousand heads and so forth.

Whatever I have said to you impetuously or by force— whether out of negligence, lack of attention, or through affectionate friendship— being ignorant of your greatness and not having experienced it myself, I now beg your forgiveness for that. I ask for your pardon.
If it is asked, "What is that? he says there: "O Kṛṣṇa," and so forth.
In the phrase *sakheti*, the sandhi is Vedic (*chāndasa*). These three vocatives contain a sense of disregard; in the case of "O Kṛṣṇa," this is because the prefix "Śrī" is absent.
In the address "O Yādava," there is the indication of an absence of belonging to the royal lineage;
in the address "O Friend" (*sakhe*), there is merely the suggestion of being of the same age.
Furthermore, whatever [insult] was offered in jest during pastimes and the like, for the sake of mockery and derision—
"If you are one whose speech is truthful, straightforward, and sincere"—thus you were insulted with such suggestive words.
"Alone," meaning either standing in a secluded place without friends, or standing in their presence while those friends were mocking you;
all that collection of offenses, whether in the form of harsh words or lack of hospitality, I beg forgiveness for: "Forgive me, O Lord, O Blessed One," thus I entreat you.
"Acyuta" means "one whose friendship does not waver" even when an offense has been committed;
[he is] "aprameya," meaning one whose power is beyond thought. //41-42//
You are the father of this world, both moving and unmoving; you are its object of worship and its most venerable teacher.
There is no one equal to you; how could there be anyone superior, even throughout the three worlds, O You of incomparable power? (43)
Śrīdhara: He states that [the Lord] possesses inconceivable power by saying "O Father.
One for whom there exists no *pratimā*—that is, no likeness or comparison—is *apratima*.
O You whose power is of such a nature, O *apratima-prabhāva* (O You of incomparable power)!

You are the father and progenitor of this world of the moving and the unmoving; therefore, you are venerable and a teacher, even more venerable and weightier than a teacher. Thus, in all the three worlds, there is indeed no other equal to you.
Since there is no other Supreme Lord, how could there possibly be anyone superior to you? //43//
Madhusūdana elaborates upon the very nature of His inconceivable power with the words "You are the father":
You are the father, the progenitor, of this world consisting of the moving and the unmoving.

You are worthy of worship because you are the Lord of all; you are a teacher because you are the instructor of the scriptures. Therefore, in every respect, you are most venerable, being weightier than any other teacher.
Therefore, there is no one equal to you; how could there be anyone superior, even in the three worlds? O You of incomparable power!

Since there is not even an equal, owing to the non-existence of a second Supreme Lord, how could there be another who is superior? The meaning is that such a thing is simply impossible in every respect. //43//
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: He states his immeasurability with the words "You are the Father.
You are the father of this world, the venerable one, the teacher, and the instructor of the scriptures.

Therefore, in every respect, you are more venerable, indeed most venerable, O You of incomparable power! Consequently, throughout this entire world-system of three realms, there is no one equal to you.
Since there is no second supreme Lord, how could there be another superior to you?
And the Śruti declares this: "Neither one equal to Him nor one superior to Him is seen. (43)
Therefore, having bowed down and prostrated my body, I seek grace from you, the Lord worthy of praise.
O Lord, as a father toward his son, as a friend toward a friend, and as a lover toward his beloved, you ought to endure this. 44.
Śrīdhara: Because it is so, therefore [he says] "therefore" (tasmāt). Therefore, to you, the Lord (īśa), the master of the world, who are worthy of praise—to you.
"I propitiate" means "I cause to be gracious.
How? Having composed the body, having prostrated like a tooth-stick; "having bowed" means having bent down completely.
Therefore, you ought to endure and forgive this great offense;
for whom and in what manner? Just as a father, out of compassion, endures the offense of his son.
A friend endures the offense of a friend, for he is a kinsman free from all conditions;
and just as a lover endures the offense of his beloved for the sake of her pleasure, so it is here. //44//
Madhusūdana: "Because it is so, therefore... means:
therefore, having bowed down—that is, having paid homage to you—having prostrated, which is to say, having held the body very low and fallen upon the ground like a staff.
I, an offender, seek to propitiate you, the Lord, the worshipful one who is praised by all.

Therefore, O God, you ought to endure and forgive my offense— just as a father forgives the offense of a son, a friend the offense of a friend, or a beloved husband the offense of his devoted wife— because I have no other refuge.
In the phrase "mama priyāyārhasi," the elision of the word *iva* and the resulting euphonic combination (*sandhi*) are Vedic. //44//
Viśvanātha:
Having prostrated himself on the ground like a staff, he said, "O beloved, you are worthy [of me]"; the sandhi here is archaic (ārṣa). //44//

Baladeva says: "Because it is thus, therefore... Having placed his body upon the ground means having prostrated, that is, having performed a full prostration with eight limbs (*sāṣṭāṅga-praṇati*). "O Lord! [he said].
"You ought to forgive my offense.
To the question "Who is like whom?", he replies, "Like a father [to his son].
However, the phrase "like a friend to a friend" is used because, upon seeing his great majesty, he considered himself a servant.
In the phrase "arhasi priyāyai," there is the elision of the visarga and the sandhi [conjunction], which are archaic (ārṣa) usages. //44//
Having seen what was never seen before, I am thrilled;
yet my mind is agitated by fear.
Show me that very form, O God;
be gracious, O Lord of Gods, O Abode of the Universe! //45//

Śrīdhara: Having thus asked for forgiveness, he prays with two verses beginning with "adṛṣṭa-pūrvam. O Lord, having seen Your form never seen before, I am thrilled—indeed, I am overjoyed—and likewise my mind is distressed and shaken by fear.
Therefore, show me that very same form to remove my distress;
O Lord of gods, O Abode of the Universe, be gracious! //45//
Madhusūdana:

Having thus prayed for forgiveness of his offense, he now prays for the vision of his former form through the withdrawal of the universal form (viśvarūpa) with two verses beginning with "adṛṣṭa-pūrvam.
Having seen the universal form never seen before—never seen previously—I am thrilled; indeed, I am overjoyed.

And my mind is distressed and agitated by the fear born from seeing that transformed form. Therefore, O God, O Lord of Gods, O Abode of the Universe, show me that very same former form which was dear to me even at the cost of my life; be gracious and grant me the favor of beholding my previous form. //45//
Viśvanātha:
Although I am thrilled at having seen this form of yours consisting of the universe, which I have never seen before, nevertheless, my mind is distressed by fear due to its terrible nature.

Therefore, be gracious and show me that very same human form, which is dearer to me than ten million lives, an ocean of sweetness, and the very appearance of the son of Vasudeva; enough for you with such sovereignty!
The meaning is: "for the purpose of seeing.
The sense of "O Lord of Gods" is: "I have realized that you alone are the sovereign of all gods and the abode of the entire universe; this is how I perceive it.

Here, at the time of the vision of the Universal Form (viśvarūpa), Arjuna did not see the dark-bodied form in human shape—which is the root of all his own forms—even though it remained right there, because it was concealed by the power of yoga-illusion (yogamāyā).
It is understood. //45//
Baladeva said: If you ask, "What do you say? What do you desire? he replies with the words beginning "adṛṣṭa" (unseen).

O Kṛṣṇa, although this divine form was known to me through my spiritual nature (*sattva*), having now seen it, I am thrilled; I am delighted because "this is the unique form of my friend," and my mind is [disturbed] by the fear born from seeing its terrible aspect.
It becomes deeply distressed;

therefore, one should pray for this very thing: "I have directly perceived that You are the Supreme Lord, the controller of all gods and the support of them all. Henceforth, including that [realization] within it, reveal to me that very form of Kṛṣṇa which is my heart's desire.
The meaning is "to cause to appear. //45//
I wish to see You likewise as before, wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and with discus in hand.
O you of universal form, become thousand-armed with that very same four-armed appearance! //46//

Śrīdhara: Specifying that very form, he says "kirīṭinam" (wearing a crown). I wish to see You as one possessing a crown, possessing a mace, and with a discus in hand—exactly as You were seen previously.
Therefore, O thousand-armed one!
O universal-formed one!
having withdrawn this universal form, manifest yourself with that very four-armed form endowed with the crown and other ornaments.
Thus, it is understood from this that Arjuna had previously seen Śrī Kṛṣṇa as already possessing a crown and other ornaments.

As for what was said earlier during the vision of the Universal Form— that "I see You wearing a crown, holding a mace, and bearing a discus"— that was intended to refer to His many crowns and other attributes.

Or rather, that very same being whom I beheld for so long a time as you—the one wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and holding a discus, and who was exceedingly gracious—I now behold as this mass of splendor difficult to look upon;
thus, there is no contradiction in the manifestation of the statement here. //46//
Madhusūdana explains that very form with the words "kirīṭinam" and so forth:
"I wish to see you thus, just as before— wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and with a discus in hand."
Therefore, appear now in that very same form with four arms as the son of Vasudeva—O thousand-armed one, O universal-formed one!
The meaning is: having withdrawn the universal form, manifest yourself again in your former form.
By this, it is stated that Arjuna always perceives the Lord in forms such as the four-armed one. //46//
Viśvanātha:
To provide further qualification, he says, "kirīṭinam" (crowned).
I wish to see you wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and with a discus in hand.
Just as you were seen before, so indeed are you now;
therefore, O thousand-armed one!
O universal-formed one!
"Having withdrawn this universal form (viśva-rūpa), appear in that very same four-armed form endowed with the crown and other ornaments.
From this it is understood that Arjuna perceived Śrī Kṛṣṇa even previously as being already endowed with the crown and the rest;
for it was stated earlier, during the vision of the universal form, that "I see You wearing a crown, holding a mace, and bearing a discus."
This is with the intention of referring to His many crowns and other ornaments;

or else, the meaning of the statement here is that "I now behold You as this mass of splendor difficult to gaze upon, who for all this time I beheld as the serene one wearing a crown, holding a mace, and bearing a discus"—thus there is no contradiction. //46//
Baladeva says: "What is that like? and thus he says, "the one wearing a diadem. O you who now possess a thousand arms!
O you whose form is the universe!
Having internalized this form, like a divine actor or dancer, manifest while distinguished by that very same four-armed form. //46//
The Blessed Lord said:
O Arjuna, because I am pleased with you, this has been shown to you.
Through my own yoga, I have shown you this supreme form—
consisting of light, universal, infinite, and primordial— which has never been seen before by anyone other than you. //47//
Śrīdhara: Thus entreated, the Blessed One, consoling him, spoke with three verses beginning with "By Me.
O Arjuna, why do you fear?
For by Me, being pleased, this supreme and most excellent form has been shown to you out of compassion.
"From my own yoga," that is, by the power of *yoga-māyā*;
he describes [the Lord] as "supreme indeed," consisting of light,
and "universal," having the universe as his self.
It is infinite and primordial;
that form of mine which has never before been seen by anyone other than you—by no devotee like yourself. //47//
Madhusūdana:

Thus entreated by Arjuna, the Blessed Lord, perceiving that Arjuna was afflicted by fear, withdrew His universal form (viśva-rūpa) and, consoling him with appropriate words, spoke in three verses beginning with "By Me": "O Arjuna, do not fear."

Since, being pleased and possessing an extraordinary compassion for you, I have shown you this supreme and most excellent form consisting of the universal manifestation through my own yoga—that is, by my unique and inherent power—I now explain its transcendence: it is composed of light, abounding in splendor; it is my entire, infinite, and primordial form, never before seen by anyone other than you, O Arjuna, Lord of the Universe!
"O Supreme Person, I desire to see your divine form"—it was solely by your request that this form of the Cosmic Person, who is a portion of Me, was shown by Me.
Why has your mind become distressed at this?
Since you say, "Be gracious, be gracious," you wish to see only My human form.
Therefore, to the question "Why do you say this is a marvel?", he replies with the word "by me":
"By me alone, being well-pleased, has this form been shown to you;
not to anyone else, because it has never before been seen by anyone other than you."
The meaning is: why is it that you do not even desire this? //47//
Baladeva: Thus requested, the Blessed One said, "By me":
"O Arjuna, I desire to show you my form," and so forth; this supreme divine form consisting of light, which you have requested, has been shown by me who am well-pleased.
This form, which is like lapis lazuli and like a master actor or a dancer, has been shown by Me to you while I abide in My desired state as Kṛṣṇa.

By My own yoga—that is, by My own inconceivable power—this form of Mine was never seen before by any person other than you. Now, through that same connection, it has been seen even by others, such as the gods; yet that essential nature of Mine remains visible only to those possessed of devotion.
In order to demonstrate to you that what was seen by me was witnessed by many, I showed this form even to the gods and others who were devoted to me.

As for the fact that the Universal Form (viśvarūpa) was also seen by Duryodhana and others at Hastināpura, that was not of such a kind; therefore, it was said that it had never been seen before by anyone other than you. //47//
Not by the study of the Vedas and sacrifices, nor by gifts,
nor by rituals, nor by fierce austerities [is this state attained].
O hero of the Kurus, it is impossible for anyone other than you to behold me in such a form in the world of men. (48)
Śrīdhara says: "Having obtained this vision which is exceedingly difficult to find, you have achieved your life's purpose. He expresses this with the words "na veda" (I do not know).
Since the study of sacrifices cannot exist apart from the study of the Vedas, the word "yajña" (sacrifice) indicates the *kalpa-sūtras* and other sciences of sacrifice.
Thus, the meaning is: "by the studies of the Vedas and the sciences of sacrifice."
Neither by gifts,
nor by ritual acts such as the Agnihotra and others,
nor by severe austerities such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and others.
In such a form as this, I can be seen by no one other than you in the world of men; rather, it is only through my grace that you have seen me and achieved your purpose. //48//

Madhusūdana says, "I do not know," meaning that having obtained My grace— which consists in the vision of this form and is exceedingly difficult to attain— you have indeed achieved your life's purpose.
This is despite the study of even the four Vedas, which consists of the grasping of syllables.
Likewise, by means of the study of the Vedas and the performance of sacrifices—namely, through the study of the Vedas and the investigation of their meaning via the Mīmāṃsā and Kalpasūtras;
through gifts such as the Tulāpuruṣa and others;
and through ritual acts such as the Agnihotra and other Śrauta rites.

O hero of the Kurus, I am not able to be seen in the world of men by anyone other than you who is devoid of my grace— nor even by those performing such fierce austerities as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*, which are difficult to perform because they wither the body and the senses.
(The elision of the visarga in "śakyo 'ham" is a Vedic [archaic] usage.)
The repetition of the word "na" (not) for each [term] is for the sake of strengthening the negation.
Furthermore, in the phrase "na ca kriyābhiḥ" (nor by actions), the particle "ca" (and) serves to include other unstated means. //48//
Viśvanātha:
He says "na veda" (no one knows) to show that this form has been revealed to you, which is difficult to attain even through the means prescribed in the Vedas and other scriptures;
for no one other than you is able to see me in such a form.
"I am capable"—
here, the elision of the dual number is archaic (ārṣa).
Therefore, considering that you have attained what was unattainable for yourself, [you should seek refuge] in this very Lord.
Fix your mind on this form, which is most difficult to obtain;
for even having seen this form, it is enough for you—there is no further desire to behold my human form. This is the intended meaning. //48//

Baladeva: Now, he states that the form of the Lord, characterized by a thousand heads and so forth, constitutes the supreme human goal, with the words "na vedānām" (not by the Vedas). This means not by the study of the Vedas—that is, by the grasping of their syllables—nor by the performance of sacrifices—that is, by the offerings made according to the Mīmāṃsā and Kalpa-sūtras.
By means of ritual acts such as the Agnihotra and other rites;
by means of severe austerities such as the Kṛcchra, which are difficult to perform because they wither the body;
and by these alone—such as the study of the Vedas and so forth—I, who am of this nature, cannot be seen by any man other than you who are endowed with devotion, that is, by anyone devoid of devotion.
Without devotion, activities such as the study of the Vedas do not become means for the vision of Me. As it has been said:
"Dharma endowed with truth and other virtues, or knowledge accompanied by austerity, does not truly purify the self if it is devoid of devotion to Me."
I have indeed been seen by you who are devoted, as well as by other devoted beings such as the gods;
for where one ought to say "I am capable" (*śakyaḥ aham*), the elision of the visarga is Vedic,
and the repetition of the letter *na* is for the purpose of emphasizing the prohibition.
By saying "in the world of men," it is implied that in that world there are many devotees of Him who are able to see Him. //48//
Let there be no fear in you, nor let there be any state of delusion,
upon seeing this terrible form of mine such as this.
Free from fear and with a joyful mind, behold once again this very form of mine. //49//

Śrīdhara: Even so, if you feel distress upon seeing this terrible form of Mine, then I shall show you that very same form; thus He says, "mā te" (let it not be for you). Let there be no distress (*vyathā*) for you (*te*) upon seeing such a terrible form of Mine as this;
and let there be no state of delusion (*vimūḍha-bhāva*), that is, no bewilderment.
Being free from fear and with a joyful mind, behold once again this very form of mine in its excellence. //49//
Madhusūdana:
May that distress—the pain caused by fear—which has arisen in you as you stand beholding this terrible form of mine, endowed with many arms and other such features, not remain;
likewise, may that state of delusion—the agitation of mind or dissatisfaction—even upon seeing my form, not remain.

But, being free from fear, with your dread departed and your mind gladdened, behold once more this very form of mine—characterized by the four arms, Vāsudeva-hood, and so forth—which was previously seen by you; behold it clearly as it is now being manifested through the withdrawal of the universal form (viśvarūpa), with freedom from fear and with joy. 49.
Viśvanātha:
O Supreme Lord,
why do you not accept me?
Since you wish to give this very thing to me by force, even though I do not desire it,
my limbs tremble upon seeing this power of yours,
and my mind becomes agitated.
I faint again and again.
To this supreme sovereignty of yours, let there be salutation after salutation from afar;
I shall never again pray to behold such a sight.
"Forgive me, forgive me!

Show me, show me that very same human form, with its face like the moon raining down the essence of nectar through a smile and laughter that bears the burden of unprecedented sweetness. To the thus agitated Arjuna, [the Lord] spoke with consolation: "Do not fear. (49)

Baladeva said: "And as for that quality of being the destroyer which was manifested by me within that very form of mine—it was indeed to make [Bhīṣma] and all the others understand that even though they remained silent upon seeing the dragging of Draupadī, they were all to be slain by me alone because I was enraged by that dragging, and that the burden of slaying them did not fall upon them; therefore, saying 'let there be no distress for you,' he meant: 'do not be distressed on their account.'"
And that very [form] has four arms, with its desired appearance. //49//
Sanjaya said:
Having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vāsudeva—
The Great-Souled One again revealed his own form and, assuming once more a gentle appearance, comforted him who was terrified. (50)
Śrīdhara: Having spoken thus, O Janārdana, I have now—this very moment—returned to my former form as your gracious and gentle friend;
that is, I have become one who is conscious and of a tranquil mind, having returned to my own nature, which is my true self. //50//
Madhusūdana—

Vāsudeva— having spoken thus to Arjuna as previously described, again showed his own four-armed form as it was before, endowed with the diadem, makara-shaped earrings, mace, discus, and other attributes, and adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha gem, a forest garland, yellow garments, and so forth.

And the Great-Souled One—the Lord of All, the Omniscient, and the source of all auspicious qualities such as supreme compassion—having again assumed his former gentle form, a body of grace, consoled the terrified Arjuna. //50//
Viśvanātha:
Just as he had shown his own portion in a most fierce form,
so too did he again show his own exceedingly sweet form— four-armed, endowed with a crown, mace, discus, and other attributes— which was requested by him and consists of sweet sovereignty.
Then again, that Great-Souled One, assuming a gentle form and becoming two-armed while wearing bracelets, earrings, a turban, and yellow garments, comforted him who was terrified. //50//
Baladeva: Then, regarding what occurred, Sañjaya spoke thus to Arjuna.

Having addressed Arjuna with what was previously stated, Vāsudeva, by his very resolve, displayed his own four-armed form—characterized as the son of Devakī and possessing qualities such as the dark hue of a blue lotus—just as he had displayed the thousand-headed form.
He manifested his form, having assumed such a gentle body and a beautiful physique; then the Great-Souled One, of noble mind, comforted the terrified Arjuna once again. //50//
Arjuna said:
O Janārdana, having seen this gentle human form of yours, [I am restored to my normal state].
Now I have become possessed of consciousness and have returned to my natural state. //51//
Śrīdhara: Then, being free from fear, Arjuna said, "Having seen this... with a conscious mind, that is, with a serene heart: "Now I have become truly composed."
I have attained my own nature and well-being;
the rest is clear. //51//
Madhusūdana:

Then, being fearless, Arjuna said, "Having seen this... Now I have become possessed of my senses (*sacetāḥ*), meaning my mind has become undisturbed due to the absence of the delusion caused by fear; likewise, I have returned to my natural state (*prakṛtim*), that is, to composure, through the absence of the distress caused by fear.
The rest is clear. //51//
Viśvanātha:

And then, having beheld Kṛṣṇa of the most sweet form and being bathed in an ocean of bliss, he said: "Just now I have become possessed of my senses; I have regained my mind, returned to my natural state, and attained composure. (51)
Baladeva: Then, freed from distress and with a serene mind, Arjuna said, "Having seen this... [He continued:

"O Janārdana, having seen this gentle and beautiful four-armed form of yours, I am now possessed of my senses; with a tranquil mind, I have returned to my natural state and attained composure through the absence of distress and other such afflictions. Thus he became.
As to what kind of form [He has], he says: "human.
Kṛṣṇa is the embodiment of consciousness and bliss, according to the scriptural and traditional texts (śruti-smṛti) that will be cited later; for He indeed [appeared] among the Yadus.
Among the Pāṇḍavas, he sometimes sports as two-armed and sometimes as four-armed;
because both of these forms possess a human-like appearance and conduct, it was previously stated that he is designated by the very status of a human being. //51//
The Blessed Lord said: You have seen this form of Mine which is very difficult to behold.
Even the gods constantly long for a vision of this form. //52//
Śrīdhara: Demonstrating the extreme rarity of the grace He has bestowed, the Blessed Lord said, "Extremely difficult to behold.
That universal form (*viśva-rūpa*) which you have seen of Mine—this is "extremely difficult to behold," meaning it is absolutely impossible to see.
For even the gods always and at all times desire the sight of this form alone;
yet they do not actually see it. //52//
Madhusūdana,
demonstrating the extreme rarity of the grace He has bestowed, the Blessed Lord spoke with the four verses beginning with "sudurdarśam":
"That form of Mine which you have now seen..."

This universal form is extremely difficult to behold, being altogether impossible to see; for even the gods have always—throughout all time—longed to see this form, but they neither saw it previously as you have, nor will they see it hereafter. This is the intended meaning, because the longing to see it is described as constant. (52)
Viśvanātha:
With three verses beginning with "sudurdarśam," he describes the majesty of the true nature (svarūpa) that has been shown.
Even the gods merely desire to behold it, but they do not obtain the vision.
But you do not even desire this;
for how could this be a theft from your eyes, which eternally relish the supreme sweetness of the human form that is my very own essential nature?
Therefore, saying "I give you divine vision," I bestowed upon him the divine eye.

However, because you have not granted a divine mind as well as a divine eye, even with your divine eye you did not perceive [this form] correctly, since your mind was focused solely on the great sweetness of my human form.
The sense is that had I also given you a divine mind, then like the gods in heaven, you too would certainly have relished this universal form, the true nature of the Supreme Person. //52//

Baladeva says: With the thought, "May Arjuna, my dear friend who has faith in my thousand-headed form— which was displayed by me and praised with words such as 'I have not seen [the like] through the study of the Vedas and sacrifices'— never again experience a lapse in his devotion toward me, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is manifested in human form," he teaches that his own form is the supreme goal of human endeavor in the verse beginning with "sudurdarśam."
My form with a thousand heads is indeed difficult to behold;
and this dark form of mine is even more difficult to see, as it has been said: "I am not manifest to everyone."
If it is asked how one can believe this, given that you have not seen it for so long, he says in response: "Even the gods [believe] this.
And this is indeed well-known from the tenth [chapter] onwards through the hymns to the Embryo (garbha-stuti) and others. //52//
Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can I be seen in such a form as you have seen Me. (11.53)
Śrīdhara: Here he states the reason: "Not I," etc. The meaning is clear. //53//
Madhusūdana says:

"Why have the gods not seen this form, or why will they not see it? [The answer is] "Because they are devoid of devotion to Me," as expressed in the verse beginning with "Not by Vedic study or sacrifices. This verse, whose meaning has already been explained, is repeated here to demonstrate that this form is supremely difficult to attain. //53//
Viśvanātha:
Furthermore, although this essential nature of yours is not something to be craved, there are others who long for it as the highest human goal;
yet even by means of such disciplines as the study of the Vedas, it is impossible for them to know or perceive it—realize this, he says with the words "Not I" (nāham). //53//
Baladeva said: "He is extremely difficult to attain; I am not such a person.
Such a son of Devakī, possessing four arms and being your friend, cannot be seen by any man devoid of devotion through any means such as the Vedas, just as you have seen me. //53//
But by unswerving devotion alone, O Arjuna, am I— such as I am— capable of being known and seen in truth, and entered into, O scorcher of the foe. (11.54)
Śrīdhara: "In that case, by what means can you be seen? To this he says: "But by devotion" (*bhaktyā tu*).

By such devotion as is directed toward me alone without any other object, I—who am thus the universal form—can be known in truth, that is, in the ultimate sense; [I can be] seen through the scriptures, seen directly, and entered into.
And it cannot be [attained] through identity, nor by other means. //54//
Madhusūdana:
If You are impossible to see through Vedic study, austerity, charity, and sacrifice, then by what means can You be seen? To this he says: "by devotion" (bhaktyā).
The word "but" (tu) is intended to exclude other means.

Only by means of exclusive devotion, through supreme love centered solely on Me, can I— who possess such a divine form— be known; yet, I can be seen in truth and realized in My essential nature through the ripening of hearing, reflecting, and meditating upon the Vedānta scriptures.

And therefore, O scorcher of foes—meaning "O subduer of the enemy that is ignorance"—I am capable of being entered by this very person only in My own form, once ignorance and its effects have ceased through the direct realization of My true nature and [the soul] has entered into reality as such. This indicates the fitness for entry. //54//
Viśvanātha:
If so, by what means is this attained? To this he says: "But by devotion" (bhaktyā tu) and "I am possible [to be known]" (śakyo ’ham).
O Vayalopa,
if there should be a desire for nirvāṇa and liberation, then it is possible to enter into the true nature of Brahman only through exclusive devotion (ananya-bhakti), and not otherwise.
Although devotion has become subordinate for the wise, at the final moment—following the renunciation of knowledge—it remains as that which is left over and becomes non-dual;
through that alone they attain *sāyujya*. We shall explain this in the passage: "Having known Me in truth, thereafter he enters [Me]" (Gītā 18.55). //54//
Baladeva, clarifying that He is visible only to His supreme devotees as desired by them, says: "By devotion.

Such a son of Devakī, I, the four-armed one, can indeed be known in reality through the Vedas and other means only by means of unswerving, exclusive devotion to Me; and I can be seen—that is, perceived directly—and entered into, and united with, in reality only through such devotion.
In the expression "entering the city," only the conjunction with the city is perceived. In this context, "Veda" refers to the Gopāla Upaniṣad;
"austerity" refers to fasting on my birthdays, such as the Aṣṭamī and Ekādaśī.
Giving (dāna) is the offering of one's own enjoyments to My devotees;
sacrifice (ijyā) is the worship of My form,
as the Veda declares in such passages as, "He who has supreme devotion for the Divine," and so forth.
The word *tu* here signifies a shift in the introductory topic.
Nor should it be said that the triad beginning with "extremely difficult to see" refers to the form with a thousand heads;
for this is immediately preceded by the two verses beginning with "Thus unto Arjuna," which concern the nature of the four-armed being in human form.
Furthermore, because there is an intervention by that pair [of verses] between [the description of] the thousand-headed form;

and because, in that case, if those [verses] were part of the same syntactical unit, it would result in the fault of redundancy for such statements as "I am not [known] by the Vedas. As for the claim that the divine form is superior to the human-like four-armed thousand-headed one—on the basis of the sign of granting divine vision—that is merely an unexamined assertion regarding that divine form.
And His true nature is indeed logical, according to the traditional teaching: "He who enjoyed the yoga-sleep within the waters of the causal ocean.

This form of Kṛṣṇa in human shape is to be understood as the all-pervading Lord, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), who is known through all the Vedāntas, and who is the source of all incarnations—[as it is said]:
"To Kṛṣṇa, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss, the performer of effortless deeds..."
Salutations to the Guru, who is to be known through Vedānta, the witness of the intellect.
Kṛṣṇa is indeed the supreme deity;
Kṛṣṇa alone is the self-controlled, all-pervading one worthy of praise.
Because of such scriptural declarations as, "Though being one, he appears as many" (GTU 1.19), and so forth:
"The Supreme Lord is Kṛṣṇa, whose form is existence-consciousness-bliss;
Govinda is without beginning, the origin, the cause of all causes" (Bs 5.1).

For it is remembered [in scripture] that "The Supreme Brahman, known as Kṛṣṇa, has descended here in human form," and "These others are but portions and fragments of the Person, but Kṛṣṇa is the Lord Himself," and so forth;
and here too, He Himself has declared: "There is nothing else higher than Me."

And [there are passages] such as "I am indeed the beginning of the gods," and by Arjuna: "The supreme Brahman, the supreme abode," and so forth. Therefore, when the vision has been transferred into that form of a thousand heads through its exceeding majesty, it is logical that the vision, having been transferred by that [form], is what perceives.
However, it should be understood that because her future vision would not be able to grasp Kṛṣṇa’s form— which is the very treasury of supreme beauty and charm—
the quality of being capable of perceiving such a form was transferred to Arjuna’s eyes, just as the quality of having a thousand heads was attributed to Kṛṣṇa’s form.
However, one should not accept the status of a mere logician by resorting to fallacious reasoning;
nor was Arjuna like other men with only physical eyes,
for he is repeatedly described in the Mahābhārata and other texts as a human incarnation of the Blessed Lord.

It has been said that through the knowledge arising from ritual action (karma), together with its subsidiaries, the thousand-headed form is attained; however, that human-shaped dark form is difficult to behold, being exceedingly hard to see through nothing other than exclusive devotion (ananya-bhakti).
O Pāṇḍava, he who performs actions for Me, who regards Me as the supreme goal, who is My devotee, who is free from attachment, and who is without enmity toward all beings— he comes to Me. 55.
Śrīdhara: Therefore, he says "one who performs my work" (*mat-karma-kṛt*), [meaning] "listen to this, which is the essence of all scriptures and the supreme secret.
One who performs action for my sake is "one who performs my work.
He for whom I alone am the supreme goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*) is [such a person].
He is my very devotee, one who has taken refuge [in me], who is free from attachment to sons and the like,
and who is without enmity toward all beings.
One who has become thus attains me, and no other. //55//
The Blessed One thus revealed his universal form to his devotee— a sight exceedingly difficult even for the gods to behold, despite millions of austerities, sacrifices, and other rites.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Vision of the Universal Form," in the *Subodhinī*, a commentary on the *Bhagavad-gītā* composed by the venerable Śrīdhara Svāmī. //11//
Madhusūdana:
Now, the essential meaning of the entire Gītā scripture is stated in summary for those seeking the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) so that they may practice it.
"One who performs actions for Me" (mat-karma-kṛt) is one who performs the action prescribed by the Vedas for My sake.
To the question, "How can this be so when there is a desire for heaven and the like? he says "no," [answering] "one who has Me as the supreme" (*mat-paramaḥ*).
This means one for whom I alone am determined to be the supreme goal to be attained, and not heaven or anything else.
For that very reason, with the hope of attaining Me, such a devotee of Mine is intent upon My worship in every way.

To the objection that this might not be possible when there is affection for sons and others, he says "no": one who is free from attachment (*saṅga-varjitaḥ*), meaning devoid of longing for external objects. To the objection that this might not be possible when there is hatred toward enemies, he says "no": one who is without enmity toward all beings (*nivairaḥ sarva-bhūteṣu*).

O Pāṇḍava, he who is free from hatred even toward those who do him harm comes to me without distinction. The meaning is that this goal which you desired to know has been taught by me; there is nothing further than this that remains to be done. //55//

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Vision of the Universal Form," in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā-gūḍhārtha-dīpikā* (The Lamp Illuminating the Hidden Meaning of the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā) composed by the disciple Śrī Madhusūdana Sarasvatī.
Viśvanātha:

Now, for the purpose of concluding the section on devotion (*bhakti-prakaraṇa*), he states the general definition of those various devotees who have been described in the seventh chapter and following, beginning with the words "one who performs my work" (*mat-karma-kṛt*).
"Free from attachment" (*saṅga-varjitaḥ*) means devoid of attachment. //55//
"Kṛṣṇa alone possesses great sovereignty, and victory in this battle belongs to me alone"—thus Arjuna resolved; this is the meaning of the chapter as it has been set forth.
Thus, in the *Harṣiṇī* commentary that showers the essence of meaning for the hearts of devotees, the eleventh chapter of the *Gītā* has been properly concluded for the virtuous. 11.
Baladeva: Now, teaching the exclusive devotion that brings about one's own attainment, he concludes with the word "mad" (me).
One who performs actions for Me is a *mat-karma-kṛt*—one who performs such acts as building My temple, cleaning it, tending My flower gardens, cultivating groves of *tulasī*, and serving them.
One for whom I am the supreme goal (*mat-parama*) is one who knows Me alone, and not heaven or other such ends of human life.
My devotee is one who delights in the ninefold nectar of devotional service, such as hearing about Me;
who is free from attachment; who cannot endure association with those averse to Me;
and who is without enmity toward all living beings.

Even when they are hostile and turned away from me, one who is free from enmity—because, by reflecting on how one's own afflictions are caused by one's own past karma, there is no basis for enmity toward them—such a person attains Me, who am Kṛṣṇa in human form; no other does. //55//
Because Kṛṣṇa has descended as Pūrṇa, there is victory in battle for his devotees;
thus, the sons of Pāṇḍu shall prevail in Bhārata—this is the determination regarding the Eleventh [Canto].
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā Upaniṣad.
